title: Wavelet-based adaptive image fusion of CT and MRI with local neighborhood variance for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
abstract: Multimodal imaging of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) requires complementary representation of CT-derived bony anatomy and MRI-derived soft-tissue contrast. Existing fusion methods may fail to preserve both structural detail and soft-tissue information in a transparent and reproducible manner. We present a wavelet-based fusion framework that employs local neighborhood variance for adaptive weighting. This interpretable variance-driven strategy selectively integrates CT bony structures and MRI soft-tissue textures according to regional information content. The neighborhood configuration was selected through an ablation analysis of 232 clinical cases. Quantitative evaluation showed improved image-quality performance over the selected comparison methods across entropy, spatial frequency, average gradient, standard deviation, and edge information preservation factor, with respective gains of approximately 5.5%, 2.4%, 6.7%, 5.1%, and 3.2% relative to the best-performing baseline for each metric. These findings support the proposed method as an image fusion methodology for preserving complementary multimodal information; direct effects on target delineation, workflow efficiency, or dosimetric outcomes require future clinical validation.

title: Breast Implant Flipping: Prevalence, Clinical Correlation, and Independent Risk Factors in a Consecutive Ultrasound Cohort.
abstract: Background Silicone breast implants are designed with an anterior domed surface, and relatively flat posterior surface that contains the cured silicone patch. With implant flipping (an anterior-posterior malposition), the posterior patch rotates to an anterior position. Objectives There are currently no prospective published studies reporting the prevalence of implant flipping and its associated symptoms in aesthetic patients. This prospective study used in-office high-resolution ultrasound (HRUS) to evaluate the prevalence of breast implant flipping, assess associated changes in breast shape, appearance, and symptoms, and identify potential risk factors. Methods Consecutive patients with silicone breast implants presenting for routine follow-up underwent HRUS at 7 study sites in the United States over a 4-month period between April 1st and August 1st, 2026. Demographic data included age and BMI. Implant data included time since surgery, whether a primary of revision procedure, number of revisions, manufacturer, size, style, surface, use of ADM or scaffold, pocket location, capsule grade, flipped or not, and rupture. Results Five hundred and ninety consecutive patients were enrolled over 4 months. Mean age 43 years with range 22-82, mean BMI 23 with range of 16-34.5. Primary augmentations accounted for 64.6% of procedures, while revision augmentations accounted for 35.4%. Device manufacturer distribution, 63.9% Allergan, 12.4% Mentor, 15.9% Motiva, and 7.1% Sientra. Implant flipping was identified in 75 patients (12.7%). Conclusions Implant flipping was identified by HRUS in one in eight patients. Larger implant volume, prepectoral placement, and lack of soft tissue support were independently associated with flipping. HRUS improves detection, patient counseling, and surgical planning.

title: Modern Radiotherapy for Axial Giant Cell Tumor of Bone: Impact of Gross Disease at Treatment Initiation.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate outcomes of modern radiotherapy (RT) for giant cell tumor of bone (GCTB) in anatomically constrained axial sites and to assess the prognostic impact of disease burden at RT initiation. Methods We retrospectively reviewed consecutive patients with pathologically confirmed GCTB of the spine, sacrum, or skull treated with RT between 2006 and 2024 at a single institution. Patients treated with palliative intent and 1 patient lost to follow-up immediately after RT were excluded. Local recurrence-free survival (LRFS) and progression-free survival (PFS) were calculated from RT initiation. Gross disease at RT was defined as a radiographically visible lesion on CT and/or MRI at RT initiation. Survival was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared by the log-rank test; prognostic factors were explored using univariate analyses. Results Seventeen patients were included (postoperative RT, n=13; salvage RT, n=3; definitive RT, n=1) and treated with 3D-conformal RT (n=9), IMRT (n=3), or proton therapy (n=5). Median follow-up was 79.8 months. The 5-year LRFS and PFS rates were 75.1% and 68.3%, respectively. Four patients experienced local recurrence and 1 developed lung metastasis. Gross disease at RT initiation (n=8) was significantly associated with inferior LRFS (5 y LRFS: 46.9% vs. 100.0% without gross disease; P=0.018). Conclusions In this cohort of axial GCTB treated with modern RT, gross disease at RT initiation was associated with inferior local control. Outcomes appeared more favorable when RT was delivered in the absence of gross disease, suggesting that maximal safe debulking before RT may be relevant in selected anatomically constrained cases.

title: Anterior Segment Ischemia and Neurotrophic Keratopathy Following Ultrasound Cycloplasty in Acute Angle-Closure Glaucoma.
abstract: Ultrasound cycloplasty (UCP) is a minimally invasive, non-incisional glaucoma procedure that has emerged in recent years and is generally associated with few complications. We report a case of a patient with acute angle-closure glaucoma underwent UCP for IOP control. She developed iris neovascularization and neurotrophic keratopathy（NK）at postoperative week 6, followed by hypopyon, flattening of the anterior chamber, and thinning of the peripheral cornea at postoperative week 11, 12, and 14, respectively. We concluded that UCP can lead to anterior segment ischemia (ASI) and NK, which manifest as iris neovascularization, painless corneal epithelial defects, peripheral corneal thinning, hypopyon, and flattening of the anterior chamber. Preoperative screening for high-risk factors is essential before performing UCP.

title: What is the Utility of Whole Body Imaging for Screening Patients With Craniofacial Fibrous Dysplasia?
abstract: Whole body imaging is commonly performed in patients with fibrous dysplasia (FD) to screen for additional lesions. However, the frequency of newly-detected lesions in patients presenting with isolated craniofacial FD is unclear. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the frequency of newly-detected FD lesions on whole body imaging in patients with craniofacial FD and no known extracraniofacial lesions or symptoms. This was a retrospective observational cohort study at a tertiary children's hospital in an urban setting. The study population consisted of patients with craniofacial FD who underwent whole body imaging with technetium-99m (Tc-99m) bone scintigraphy or fluorine-18 sodium fluoride positron emission tomography/computed tomography (F-18 NaF PET/CT). Patients with previously identified extracraniofacial lesions, symptoms, or McCune-Albright syndrome were excluded. The primary outcome was the frequency of newly-detected extracraniofacial FD lesions. Fifteen subjects were included (80% female). Mean age at FD diagnosis was 9.6±4.3 years, and mean age at imaging was 10.4±4.2 years. Tc-99m bone scintigraphy was the most common imaging modality (86.7%). Newly-detected extracraniofacial FD lesions were observed in 1 of 15 subjects (6.7%). Two additional subjects (13.3%) had incidental skeletal findings related to recent traumatic injuries. In patients presumed to have isolated craniofacial FD, whole body imaging identified a low frequency of extracraniofacial skeletal lesions. These findings suggest that routine screening may be considered selectively based on clinical history and physical examination. Further investigation is required to develop evidence-based screening guidelines.

title: In older adults, "mild" by GCS does not mean low risk: Multicenter study of 1,157 patients with mild TBI and acute subdural hematoma.
abstract: Background Acute traumatic subdural hematoma (SDH) is the most common intracranial injury in mild TBI (mTBI), particularly in older adults. However, the relationship of patient and brain computed tomography (CT) characteristics with outcomes remains poorly described in a contemporary cohort. This study aims to characterize outcomes in younger and older adults with mTBI and isolated acute SDH. Methods This was a 10-center, retrospective cohort study of adult traumas with emergency department Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) 13 to 15 and acute traumatic SDH on initial brain CT ('22-'23). Trauma registry, EHR, and Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS) data were collected through automated and manual methods. The primary outcome was total mortality (TM=death+hospice discharge); the sample was stratified by 18 to 64 versus older than or equal to 65 years. Multivariable backward selection logistic regression examined 21 demographic, injury, and brain CT covariates. Results In total, 1,157 patients were included (18-64 y: 28%; ≥65 y: 72%; 58% transferred in). Median [IQR] non-head ISS was 1 [1-5] in 18 to 64 years, and 1 [1-2] in older than or equal to 65 years. Ten percent had neurosurgical intervention (18-64 y: 8%; ≥65 y: 11%). TM was higher in older than or equal to 65 years than 18 to 64 years (10% vs. 3%). Compared with older than or equal to 65 years, 18 to 64 years were discharged home more frequently (78% vs. 51%) and to hospice less frequently (2% vs. 7%). In 18 to 64 years, factors associated with TM were race, advance directive, functional dependence, ISS, more midline shift, and thicker SDH (too few TMs for adjusted models). In older than or equal to 65 years, factors independently associated with TM were advance directive (aOR [95% CI]: 11.8 [2.9-49.0]), male sex (3.0 [1.3-7.0]), midline shift (1.8 [1.3-2.6]), shock index (1.5 [1.1-2.1]), and worsening SDH on follow-up CT (2.9 [1.3-6.6]). Conclusions Despite presenting as "mild", these data highlight that older adults with SDH have high TM and should continue to receive the highest-level care with timely goals-of-care discussions. The association between advance directives and TM should be interpreted within the context of baseline vulnerability and preinjury treatment preferences, not as a biological mortality predictor. Level of evidence Level III, prognostic/epidemiological.

title: Noise2Match: Self-Supervised Low-Dose CT Denoising via Adaptive Inter-Slice Matching.
abstract: With the rapid development of deep learning, supervised convolutional neural network methods have greatly improved the performance of low-dose computed tomography (CT) denoising. However, they require paired noisy-clean training data, which is difficult to obtain in practice. Some classic self-supervised denoising methods rely on the assumption of pixel-wise independent noise, making them ineffective for correlated noise in low-dose CT (LDCT) images. Considering the high similarity and weaker noise correlation between adjacent CT slices, several recently proposed self-supervised methods use adjacent LDCT slices for training. Nevertheless, these approaches fail to effectively account for the non-rigid mis-alignment between slices caused by anatomical variation, hindering them from satisfying the equal-mean condition required by the classic Noise2Noise framework. In this paper, we propose Noise2Match, a self-supervised LDCT denoising method based on adaptive inter-slice matching. Noise2Match introduces an inter-slice matching network to model the label transition process between adjacent slices, and then applies correction to the denoiser's outputs to better satisfy the equal-mean condition. We theoretically prove that, under idealized conditions, training Noise2Match using adjacent LDCT slices is equivalent to supervised training with paired noisy-clean images. We further find that Noise2Match can also effectively perform low-dose cone-beam CT (CBCT) denoising, which could be attributed to its correction operation that reduces inter-slice noise correlation. To the best of our knowledge, Noise2Match is the first effective image-domain self-supervised method for low-dose CBCT. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Noise2Match outperforms existing image-domain self-supervised methods, offering broader applicability and higher practical value.

title: Integrating Plain 2D Ultrasound and Clinical Data for Identification of At-Risk MASH: A Multicenter Proof of Concept Study.
abstract: Background Identifying people with at-risk metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is a major challenge. We aimed to use deep learning to develop a convolutional neural network (CNN) model to facilitate the detection of at-risk MASH. Methods A multi-center cohort study was conducted across five tertiary hospitals in Japan and China. Clinical data and conventional ultrasound images were retrospectively collected. Organ segmentation using YOLO version 11 with quality control was performed, followed by creation of an EfficientNet-B6 CNN regression model, with image-level predictions averaged per patient, to estimate FAST and AGILE 3+ risk categories. Model performance was assessed using agreement across clinically relevant rule-out and rule-in thresholds, R 2 , root mean squared error (RMSE), and area under the receiver operating curve (AUROC). Results The final dataset comprised 416 patients for training (7643 images), 139 for internal validation (2463 images), and 154 for external testing (3539 images). The CNN model demonstrated good agreement with FAST (R 2 = 0.684; RMSE = 0.131; category agreement = 0.71) and moderate agreement with AGILE 3+ (R 2 = 0.445; RMSE = 0.1964; category agreement = 0.63). For FAST, AUROC was 0.974 (95% CI 0.947-0.993) for 0.35 and 0.932 (95% CI 0.884-0.969) for the 0.67 cut-off. For AGILE 3+, AUROC was 0.908 (95% CI 0.854-0.950) for 0.451 and 0.902 (95% CI 0.839-0.953) for the 0.679 cut-off. Conclusion The CNN model applied to clinical ultrasound images can approximate the accuracy of VCTE-based composite risk scores for detecting at-risk MASH. This may support the detection of at-risk MASH in settings with limited access to transient elastography.

title: Comparison Between Interlaminar and Transforaminal Endoscopic Lumbar Discectomy for Sciatic Scoliosis Secondary to Lumbar Disc Herniation: A Retrospective Study With a Minimum 1 Year Follow-Up.
abstract: Objective This study aims to compare the clinical and radiographic outcomes of interlaminar and transforaminal endoscopic lumbar discectomy (IELD and TELD) in the treatment of lumbar disc herniation (LDH) with sciatic scoliosis. Methods Patients with sciatic scoliosis secondary to LDH who had undergone IELD or TELD between January 2022 to June 2024 were reviewed. Radiographic parameters, including Cobb angle, apical vertebral translation (AVT), and coronal balance distance (CBD), were measured preoperatively and postoperatively to assess curve evolution. Clinical outcomes were evaluated using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) and the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI). Meanwhile, perioperative data were also collected. Comparisons between the groups were made by independent t-tests and χ 2 tests. Results A total of 134 patients in the IELD group and 103 patients in the TELD group were included in this study. There was no significant difference in intraoperative blood loss (13.4 ± 7.8 mL vs. 11.5 ± 7.1 mL, p = 0.067) and postoperative length of stay (2.5 ± 0.6 days vs. 2.5 ± 0.8 days, p = 0.378) between the two groups; however, the IELD group demonstrated shorter operation time (87.2 ± 17.4 min vs. 96.1 ± 23.3 min, p = 0.001) and fewer intraoperative fluoroscopy times (4.9 ± 0.7 vs. 10.3 ± 2.7, p < 0.001) compared to the TELD group. Both groups showed significant improvements in VAS and ODI scores (p < 0.05), with no significant differences between the groups. Before surgery, 86.9% (206/237) patients had a disc herniation at the convex side of the lumbosacral curve and 86.5% (205/237) patients showed a trunk shift toward the opposite side of disc herniation. After surgery, 91.8% (123/134) of the IELD group and 90.3% (93/103) of the TELD group achieved resolution of scoliosis (AVT ≤ 10 mm) within 12 months. At the final follow-up, the AVT, Cobb angle, CBD, and SVA in the IELD group were 2.7 ± 2.0 mm, 1.0° ± 0.8°, 1.2 ± 0.9 mm, and 3.4 ± 3.1 mm, respectively, with no significant differences compared to the 2.8 ± 2.7 mm, 1.1° ± 0.8°, 1.2 ± 0.8 mm, and 3.7 ± 3.5 mm in the TELD group. Conclusions Both IELD and TELD are effective and safe for LDH with sciatic scoliosis, with comparable radiographic and clinical outcomes in terms of scoliosis correction. IELD is associated with shorter operation time and fewer intraoperative fluoroscopy times in this cohort.

title: Amyloid-β Immunotherapy in Alzheimer's Disease: Challenges and Opportunities.
abstract: Passive anti-amyloid-β immunotherapy has shifted from repeated phase 3 failure to reproducible, although modest, clinical slowing in biomarker-defined early Alzheimer's disease. We review lessons from first-generation antibodies, including inadequate target engagement, late-stage enrollment, and limited outcome sensitivity. We then compare second-generation agents (i.e., aducanumab, lecanemab, and donanemab) highlighting amyloid-β species selectivity, plaque clearance kinetics, and durability, and we discuss emerging delivery innovations. Safety is dominated by amyloid-related imaging abnormalities, likely reflecting cerebrovascular amyloid vulnerability, and requires timely baseline magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) screening; APOE -informed counseling; and standardized, front-loaded MRI surveillance with symptom-triggered evaluation. We summarize prevention trials in autosomal dominant and sporadic preclinical populations and consider prospects for combination or sequential regimens with tau-targeting therapies. Finally, we focus on biomarker-guided implementation: blood-based prescreening, confirmation pathways, monitoring of biological response, and treat-to-clear or stopping concepts, alongside unresolved issues of health-system readiness, equity, and budget impact. Registry-enabled learning is emphasized to generate real-world safety and effectiveness evidence.

title: Next-Generation Sequencing to Identify Genetic Causes of Chinese Patients Affected With Non-retinal Developmental Eye Disorders.
abstract: To investigate the genetic causes of non-retinal developmental eye disorders in 14 Chinese different families, we subjected participants to a specific hereditary eye disease enrichment panel (HEDEP) or whole exome sequencing. We further validated disease-causing variants and performed co-segregation analyses on the available family members by Sanger sequencing. We classified sequence changes according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics and the Association for Molecular Pathology variant interpretation guidelines. Fourteen probands with diverse clinical diagnoses were analyzed, including microphthalmia (with or without microcornea and congenital cataract or congenital corneal opacification (CCO), four cases), anterior segment dysgenesis (ASD, six cases)-including Peter's anomaly (PA, one case), PA and microphthalmia (one case), iridocoloboma or aniridia (with microcornea and/or congenital cataract, two cases), and primary congenital glaucoma (PCG, two cases)-congenital cataract (with CCO or microcornea, three cases), and Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome (RSTS, one case). Initial inheritance patterns for 1, 5, and 8 cases were autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant, and sporadic, respectively. We identified 17 (likely) pathogenic variants and one variant of uncertain significance (VUS) in 16 genes, including BMP4 , BCOR , PITX3 , and PAX6 . Among them, eight were novel variants, and two were de novo . We confirmed the pathogenicity of PAX6 intronic mutation using in vitro splice assays and redefined the pathogenicity of the variants of uncertain significance as likely pathogenic. Patients with developmental eye diseases typically have complex ocular and systemic phenotypes, possibly leading to significant visual impairment and high blindness rates. Identifying the genetic causes facilitates early diagnosis and effective treatment and rehabilitation strategies, thereby providing valuable insights for genetic and clinical counseling of these patients.

title: Guidelines for Colonic Diverticular Disease-2026, Second Edition: Management of Diverticular Bleeding and Acute Diverticulitis.
abstract: Colonic diverticular disease is becoming increasingly common in Japan, paralleling population aging and changes in lifestyle and medication use. The predominance of right-sided diverticulosis in Asian populations, in contrast to the left-sided predominance in Western populations, influences clinical presentation and management. In Japan, diverticulitis has become a clinically important problem, and diverticular bleeding is currently the most frequent cause of acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB). The Japanese Gastroenterological Association updated its clinical guidelines for diverticular bleeding and diverticulitis in 2026. Key domains including epidemiology, diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, and priority clinical and future research questions were addressed. Evidence was graded using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach, and recommendations were formulated via a modified Delphi process with external review. These guidelines aim to provide Japanese and Asian evidence-based consensus that complements Western guidelines. Recommendations for acute LGIB and diverticular bleeding are as follows: risk stratification with the Shock Index and Oakland and NOBLADS scores guides triage; pre-colonoscopy contrast-enhanced computed tomography is the widely used diagnostic modality; routine colonoscopy within 24 h is not suggested for all patients; endoscopic band ligation or direct clipping is suggested post-detection of stigmata of recent hemorrhage; and early oral refeeding is suggested. Recommendations for diverticulitis are as follows: post-resolution colonoscopy is suggested to exclude colorectal cancer; outpatient treatment and withholding of antibiotics are suggested in selected uncomplicated cases; and primary anastomosis may be favored over Hartmann's procedure in selected complicated cases.

title: Residual Cardiovascular Risk Beyond Coronary Physiology: Complementary Prognostic Value of Trimethylamine N-Oxide in Patients Undergoing Coronary Computed Tomography Angiography With Computed Tomography-Derived Fractional Flow Reserve.
abstract: Background Coronary computed tomography (CT) angiography with CT-derived fractional flow reserve (CT-FFR) enables noninvasive identification of flow-limiting coronary stenosis and is widely used for risk assessment. However, adverse cardiovascular events still occur in a subset of patients without functionally significant ischemia, suggesting that physiological assessment alone may not fully capture patient-level risk. We aimed to evaluate whether circulating trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), a gut microbiota-derived biomarker, provides complementary prognostic information. Methods In this biobank-linked retrospective cohort study, 3978 patients undergoing clinically indicated coronary CT angiography with CT-FFR assessment were included. Serum TMAO concentrations were measured from cryopreserved samples obtained within ±30 days of imaging. Patients were stratified into high and low TMAO groups according to the receiver operating characteristic-derived threshold. The primary end point was major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events during a median follow-up of ∼3 years. Multivariable Cox models evaluated associations between TMAO and outcomes, and incremental prognostic value beyond clinical variables and CT-FFR was assessed. Results Event rates were similar across physiological strata (10.6% for CT-FFR ≤0.80 versus 10.0% for CT-FFR >0.80), indicating outcome heterogeneity beyond ischemia status. Higher TMAO levels were independently associated with major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events after adjustment for clinical covariates and CT-FFR (hazard ratio, 1.82 [95% CI, 1.44-2.31]; P <0.001). Addition of TMAO improved discrimination after bootstrap optimism correction (C-index 0.552-0.591). Among patients with preserved CT-FFR, elevated TMAO identified a subgroup with higher event rates, whereas patients with preserved CT-FFR and low TMAO had the most favorable prognosis. Conclusions Physiological assessment and clinical outcomes are not synonymous in patients undergoing coronary CT angiography. Circulating TMAO provides complementary prognostic information and refines risk stratification, particularly among individuals without functionally significant ischemia. Integrating systemic biomarkers with coronary physiological assessment may improve individualized risk evaluation beyond imaging alone.

title: Assessing the reliability of hippocampal single-voxel proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy through intra-class effect decomposition.
abstract: The hippocampus is crucial for learning, memory, and stress regulation, but is vulnerable to influences that compromise its structural and metabolic integrity. Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) enables in vivo quantification of hippocampal neurochemistry, yet the absolute and relative reliability of these measures has rarely been systematically evaluated. We assessed hippocampal metabolite estimates acquired with single-voxel MRS using a semi-adiabatic localization by adiabatic selective refocusing (semi-LASER) sequence at 3 T. Nineteen healthy adults (8 male; mean age = 40.9 ± 16.9 years) underwent four measurements across 2 consecutive days, with one session including an extended acquisition. Absolute reliability was quantified using within-subject coefficients of variation (CVs), and relative reliability was estimated with the Intra-Class Effect Decomposition (ICED) framework, which partitions variance into true-score, day-specific, session-specific, and residual components. Despite good spectral quality and high absolute reliability for several metabolites, relative reliability ranged from poor to good. Good relative reliability was observed only for water-referenced myo-inositol, total choline, and total creatine; no creatine-referenced metabolite reached this threshold. Increasing the number of transients increased signal-to-noise ratio but did not improve relative reliability; only creatine-referenced total N-acetylaspartate showed significant session-specific variance. Thus, high absolute reliability did not necessarily imply high relative reliability. Hippocampal MRS at 3 T may, therefore, be suitable for group-level or mean-level metabolite estimates, but appears less suitable for correlational, biomarker, or other individual-difference applications that require stable between-person differences. Methodological refinement, including improved voxel placement, motion correction, shimming, and quantification pipelines, may improve the relative reliability of hippocampal MRS.

title: Sex differences and prevalence of prior deep vein thrombosis among patients with incidental iliac vein compression on computed tomography.
abstract: PurposeThe purpose of this study was to identify risk factors and evaluate clinical outcomes associated with incidental left common iliac vein compression on CT imaging.MethodsThis is a retrospective study that reviewed venous-phase abdomen and pelvis CT scans to identify patients with incidental extrinsic compression of the left common iliac vein due to an overlying right common iliac artery. A total of 726 patients were included (364 females, 362 males; mean patient age: 61.9 ± 15.9 years). Board-certified radiologists reviewed all CT scans. Significant left iliac vein compression was defined as >50% luminal narrowing.ResultsSignificant iliac vein compression was identified in 114 (15.7%) patients and was more common in females (19.5%) versus males (11.9%) ( p < 0.01). Patients with iliac vein compression >50% had significantly lower BMI than those without compression (24.8 ± 6.2 vs 28.7 ± 7.2 kg/m 2 , p < 0.01). Patients with incidental left iliac vein compression had a higher rate of prior left lower extremity DVT ( p = 0.02).ConclusionIncidental left common iliac vein compression was present in approximately 16% of patients and was more frequent among females. Compression was associated with lower BMI and more than twice the rate of ipsilateral DVT, despite no prior diagnosis of MTS. These findings suggest that incidental iliac vein compression could have more clinical significance than previously recognized.

title: Use of plasma chromogranin a epitopes vasostatin and catestatin as biomarkers for catecholamine-producing tumours in dogs.
abstract: Background Differentiation of catecholamine-producing tumours from other adrenal tumours remains difficult. Chromogranin A (CgA) is a marker for catecholamine secretion in the body. An assay for quantification of the CgA epitopes vasostatin and catestatin has been validated for use in dogs but not yet evaluated in dogs with catecholamine-producing tumours. The aims were to evaluate the assays foranalysis of plasma concentrations of the CgA epitopes vasostatin and catestatin in dogs with adrenal tumours and to compare concentrations between catecholamine-producing tumours and adrenocortical tumours in dogs that were subjected to adrenalectomy. Twelve dogs with histopathologically confirmed catecholamine-secreting tumours (eleven pheochromocytomas (PCCs), one extra-adrenal sympathetic paraganglioma (PGL)) and twelve with adrenocortical tumours were included in the study. Plasma concentrations of the CgA epitopes vasostatin and catestatin were determined byradioimmunoassay (RIA), before adrenalectomy in 23 out of 24 dogs and after adrenalectomy in six of the dogs with catecholamine-secreting tumours (five PCC, one PGL). Tumour diagnosis was made by histopathology in all cases. Results Overall, median plasma concentration of the CgA epitopevasostatin in dogs with catecholamine-secreting tumours was 0.82 nmol/L (interquartile range (IQR) 0.52 to 1.60 nmol/L), which was significantly higher(Wilcoxon rank sum exact test, P= 0.0374) than the vasostatin concentration in adrenocortical tumours (median 0.50; IQR 0.34 to 0.59 nmol/L). A subsetof dogs (5/12) with catecholamine-secreting tumours had elevated plasma vasostatin concentrations preoperatively. After successful surgery, thepreoperatively elevated plasma vasostatin concentrations decreased numerically, however without reaching statistical significance. Catestatin concentrationdid not differ between tumour types. Conclusions Elevated plasma concentration of the CgA epitope vasostatin showed potential as a biomarker for asubset of catecholamine-secreting tumours.

Background

Differentiation of catecholamine-producing tumours from other adrenal tumours remains difficult. Chromogranin A (CgA) is a marker for catecholamine secretion in the body. title: Large language model assistance for report-based carotid plaque AHA classification: a multi-reader study.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate whether large language model assistance improves radiologists' agreement with a text-based reference standard in inferring the modified American Heart Association carotid plaque classification from free-text MRI reports, and whether a lightweight model can perform well under criteria-guided prompting. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 433 patients from three institutions. In a report-based reader study, four radiologists classified MRI reports with and without large language model assistance. In standalone evaluation, a rule-based baseline and 10 models were compared under naive and criteria-guided prompting. The reference standard was expert consensus based on the report text. Results Among 433 patients (mean age, 65.9 years ± 13.4; 248 males), AI assistance improved six-class agreement with the text-based reference standard. At the vessel level, junior radiologists improved from 61.75% to 83.12% (Qwen3-8B) and 87.75% (DeepSeek-R1); senior radiologists from 77.00% to 87.50% and 92.25%, respectively (all Holm-corrected p < 0.001). Patient-level agreement increased from 41.0% to 78.8% (junior) and from 59.8% to 87.8% (senior) with DeepSeek-R1. Agreement increased (quadratic-weighted κ: 0.231 without AI vs 0.775 with DeepSeek-R1). In standalone evaluation, criteria-guided prompting improved Qwen3-8B agreement from 38.91% to 81.52% (95% CI: 78.87-84.06%), remaining 5.89 percentage points below DeepSeek-R1 (87.41%; 95% CI: 85.10-89.61%). Conclusion In this report-based classification setting, large language model assistance improved radiologists' agreement with the text-based reference standard, with larger gains in junior radiologists. When prompts explicitly encoded AHA criteria, an 8B local candidate model performed well, supporting its potential use as a standardization aid for text-based workflows. Key points Question Report-based modified AHA classification of carotid plaques is experience-dependent and difficult to standardize, as mapping multi-sequence imaging findings to classification conclusions imposes substantial cognitive load. Findings Large language model assistance improved agreement with a text-based reference standard and raised inter-reader consistency (weighted κ 0.231-0.775), narrowing the junior-senior gap. Critical relevance statement Embedding explicit AHA criteria in the prompt let an 8B model approach 671B-model agreement (38.91-81.52%), supporting standardized text-based workflows without fine-tuning.

title: Multimodal imaging features of nuclear protein in testis carcinoma of the submandibular gland: a case report.
abstract: Rationale NUT carcinoma (NC) is a rare and highly aggressive malignancy defined by rearrangements of the NUTM1gene. Primary NC of the submandibular gland is exceptionally rare, with nonspecific imaging features that often lead to misdiagnosis as common salivary gland tumors and delayed treatment. Patient concerns A 32-year-old man presented with a painless mass in the left submandibular region that rapidly enlarged from 2 cm to approximately 4 cm within 1 month, accompanied by the development of ipsilateral pharyngeal and periauricular pain. Diagnoses Preoperative multimodal imaging-computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)-revealed an ill-defined, invasive mass with heterogeneous enhancement and intense metabolic activity (SUVmax 18.4). The diagnosis was confirmed by histopathological examination and immunohistochemical analysis, which demonstrated diffuse nuclear positivity for NUT protein. Interventions The patient underwent radical surgical resection (left neck dissection), followed by adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Outcomes No evidence of local recurrence or metastatic disease was observed on follow-up imaging at 9 months postoperatively. Lessons This case underscores that although the imaging features of submandibular gland NC are not pathognomonic, the combination of a rapidly growing invasive mass, heterogeneous enhancement, and marked hypermetabolism should raise clinical suspicion. Prompt biopsy with NUT immunohistochemical testing is essential for definitive diagnosis and early intervention, which is critical given the tumor's highly aggressive nature.
originalAbstract:
Rationale

NUT carcinoma (NC) is a rare and highly aggressive malignancy defined by rearrangements of the NUTM1gene. Primary NC of the submandibular gland is exceptionally rare, with nonspecific imaging features that often lead to misdiagnosis as common salivary gland tumors and delayed treatment.

Patient concerns

A 32-year-old man presented with a painless mass in the left submandibular region that rapidly enlarged from 2 cm to approximately 4 cm within 1 month, accompanied by the development of ipsilateral pharyngeal and periauricular pain.

Diagnoses

Preoperative multimodal imaging-computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT)-revealed an ill-defined, invasive mass with heterogeneous enhancement and intense metabolic activity (SUVmax 18.4). The diagnosis was confirmed by histopathological examination and immunohistochemical analysis, which demonstrated diffuse nuclear positivity for NUT protein.

Interventions

The patient underwent radical surgical resection (left neck dissection), followed by adjuvant chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

Outcomes

No evidence of local recurrence or metastatic disease was observed on follow-up imaging at 9 months postoperatively.

Lessons

This case underscores that although the imaging features of submandibular gland NC are not pathognomonic, the combination of a rapidly growing invasive mass, heterogeneous enhancement, and marked hypermetabolism should raise clinical suspicion. Prompt biopsy with NUT immunohistochemical testing is essential for definitive diagnosis and early intervention, which is critical given the tumor's highly aggressive nature.

title: Fully automated diaphragm segmentation on routine 2D-cine and 3D thoracic MRI: multireader validation.
abstract: Objective The diaphragm is central to respiratory mechanics and may be impaired in various diseases. Parametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment is limited by time-consuming manual segmentation. We developed and validated fully automated diaphragm segmentation on two-dimensional (2D)-cine and three-dimensional (3D) thoracic MRI. Materials and methods In this single-center study, eligible adults without known diaphragmatic disorders underwent 2D-cine MRI, 3D MRI, or both. Two U-Net models (2D/3D) were trained using expert manual contours as ground truth. Performance was evaluated with normalized surface Dice (NSD) with 3-voxel tolerance and average surface distance (ASSD). In the main cohort, five blinded radiologists rated segmentation usability and image quality. An additional separate pathology cohort was assessed by two blinded readers using the same scale. Results Overall, 59 individuals contributed 70 MRI acquisitions: 29 women, 30 men; aged 49.3 ± 18.8 years (mean ± standard deviation). Inference required 5 s (2D) and 30 s (3D) versus 10 min and 4.5 h for manual annotation. Segmentation accuracy was high: NSD 0.95 ± 0.08 (2D) and 0.92 ± 0.06 (3D), with ASSD 1.97 ± 2.29 mm (2D) and 1.88 ± 1.97 mm (3D). In the main cohort, segmentations were rated clinically usable in 87.5% (2D) and 100% (3D). Mean image-quality scores were 4.0/5 (2D) and 4.2/5 (3D) and correlated with segmentation quality. In the pathology cohort (n = 5), segmentation usability for 2D images was 75% for reader 1 and 70% for reader 2 for 2D images and 80% for both readers for 3D volumes. Conclusion Automated diaphragm segmentation on 2D-cine and 3D MRI is feasible, accurate, and time-efficient, supporting scalable, standardized diaphragm analysis as a basis for deriving diaphragm biomarkers. Key points Question Can fully automated diaphragm segmentation make routine 2D-cine and 3D thoracic MRI analysis clinically feasible by replacing time-consuming manual delineation? Findings Automated segmentation achieved normalized surface Dice above 0.9, radiologist acceptability in 87.5-100% of cases, and inference times below 30 s Relevance statement Automated diaphragm segmentation on routine 2D-cine and 3D static MRI yields accurate, radiologist-acceptable segmentations with normalized surface Dice exceeding 0.9 and mean surface deviations below 2 mm. This approach may support standardized diaphragm assessment for objective quantification in thoracic and neuromuscular imaging pending larger multicenter validation.

In this single-center study, eligible adults without known diaphragmatic disorders underwent 2D-cine MRI, 3D MRI, or both. Two U-Net models (2D/3D) were trained using expert manual contours as ground truth. Performance was evaluated with normalized surface Dice (NSD) with 3-voxel tolerance and average surface distance (ASSD). title: Diagnostic challenges of masked arginine vasopressin deficiency in neurosarcoidosis complicated by sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor use.
abstract: A wide variety of endocrine disorders caused by sarcoidosis have been reported to date. We report the case of an 82-year-old male patient who presented with hypercalcemia and anterior pituitary hormone deficiency at the time of his sarcoidosis diagnosis and was subsequently diagnosed with arginine vasopressin deficiency (AVP-D) 6 months after the initiation of glucocorticoid therapy. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed an enlarged pituitary gland, thickened pituitary stalk, and loss of the posterior pituitary bright spot, raising the suspicion of hypothalamic-pituitary sarcoidosis. Despite improvement in hypercalcemia, anterior pituitary function, and pituitary enlargement and stalk thickening with glucocorticoid therapy, subjective symptoms of dry mouth and polyuria gradually became apparent several months after the start of treatment. While the characteristic hypotonic polyuria of AVP-D was not prominent, we surmised that these typical clinical features were masked by adrenal insufficiency, chronic kidney disease (CKD), and concurrent use of a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor for type 2 diabetes. This case highlights the fact that the typical presentation of AVP-D can be masked by concurrent SGLT2 inhibitor use and CKD, emphasizing careful assessment of water balance in such patients.

title: White Matter Functional Disconnection Predicts Long-Term Disability and Early Mortality in Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
abstract: Background and objectives Spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) has the highest short-term mortality among stroke subtypes, and progress in treatment has been hindered by the limited accuracy of current prognostic tools. We investigated whether white matter functional disconnection severity, estimated using a normative lesion network mapping framework integrating direct electrical stimulation and resting-state functional MRI data from previously published independent Data sets, improves prediction of 6-month functional outcome measured with the modified Rankin Scale (mRS). Methods We analyzed 97 patients with spontaneous ICH. Ordinal logistic regression models were used to evaluate the association between domain-specific disconnection severity and 6-month mRS, and to compare traditional functional outcome in patients with primary intracerebral hemorrhage and ICH scores with connectivity-enriched models incorporating disconnection measures. Results White matter functional disconnectivity was significantly associated with 6-month functional outcome (mRS; P < .001; Nagelkerke's R2 = 0.507). Integrating disconnection severity into the functional outcome in patients with primary intracerebral hemorrhage and ICH scores improved predictive performance in both cases (Nagelkerke's R2 = 0.615 vs 0.389 and 0.651 vs 0.434, respectively), with the connectivity-enriched ICH score achieving the strongest overall fit across all models tested. Exploratory analyses showed associations between domain-specific disconnection severity, residual functional deficits, and early mortality. Conclusion Assessment of white matter functional disconnection severity seems to be a promising approach for predicting long-term disability after ICH, although prospective validation in larger multicenter cohorts is required before clinical implementation. The findings suggest that different brain networks exhibit variable vulnerability to injury and differential potential for functional recovery.

title: Large Carinal Chondrosarcoma: Resection of the Main Carina, Distal Trachea, and Orifices of the Mainstem Bronchi and Construction of a New Carina.
abstract: BACKGROUND Chondrosarcoma of the trachea is an extremely rare malignancy, and tumors located at the main carina are even rarer. Carinal resection and subsequent reconstruction of a new carina constitute a demanding surgical procedure that requires extensive expertise and close collaboration between the anesthetic and surgical teams. In this case report, we aim to highlight the rarity of chondrosarcoma of the main carina and emphasize the critical role of surgical intervention despite the complexity of the procedure. Furthermore, we aim to share our clinical experience and contribute an additional case to the limited literature. CASE REPORT A 23-year-old man presented with dyspnea, fatigue, and cough. Chest computed tomography showed a lobulated soft-tissue mass anterior to the distal trachea and main carina. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy revealed widening of the main carina, clinically significant stenosis of the mainstem bronchi, and mucosal infiltration. Biopsy specimens obtained via mediastinoscopy demonstrated well-differentiated carinal chondrosarcoma. Through a right posterolateral thoracotomy, the distal trachea, main carina, and orifices of the mainstem bronchi were resected. A new carina was constructed and anastomosed to the distal trachea. Gross examination of the surgical specimen showed a well-circumscribed mass with a lobulated external surface measuring 7×6.5×5 cm. The patient remains well 17 years after tumor resection, without signs of recurrence. CONCLUSIONS Chondrosarcoma involving the distal trachea and main carina is an extremely rare tumor. Given the limited efficacy of chemotherapy and radiotherapy, surgical resection with reconstruction of a new carina is the primary treatment.

title: Histopathologic spectrum of focal liver lesions diagnosed by ultrasound-guided percutaneous liver biopsy and predictors of hepatocellular carcinoma: A single-center experience from Sub-Saharan Africa.
abstract: Background Focal liver lesions (FLLs) encompass a wide spectrum of benign and malignant pathologies, and accurate diagnosis is essential for appropriate management. Although advances in imaging have improved lesion characterization, histopathologic assessment remains the diagnostic gold standard for indeterminate lesions. Data on the histopathologic spectrum and diagnostic utility of ultrasound-guided percutaneous liver biopsy (US-PLB) in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) are limited. This study aimed to characterize the histopathologic findings of US-PLB performed for FLLs at a tertiary referral center in SSA and to identify factors associated with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Methods We conducted a retrospective observational study of adult patients (≥18 years) who underwent US-PLB for FLL between January 2021 and December 2024 at Adera Medical and Surgical Center. Patients with indeterminate pathology results, incomplete records, biopsies performed for diffuse liver disease, or lesions classified as LI-RADS 1, 2, or 5 were excluded. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, imaging, histopathologic, and outcome data were extracted from medical records. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize patient characteristics and histopathologic diagnoses. Logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with HCC. Results A total of 119 were included in the final analysis. The median age was 56 years (IQR 45-65), and 59.7% were male. The median focal liver lesion size was 8.20 cm (IQR: 5.1-11.0 cm), with 38.7% presenting as multifocal lesions. No major biopsy-related complications were reported. HCC was the most common histopathologic diagnosis, accounting for 42.9% of cases, followed by secondary metastatic tumors (15.9%) and regenerative nodules (15.9%). Other diagnoses included chronic hepatitis (8.4%), cholangiocarcinoma (5.9%), and hepatic abscess (3.4%). Hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections were present in 14.3% and 12.4% of patients, respectively. On multivariate analysis, HBV infection (AOR 7.85, 95% CI 1.45-42.60; p = 0.017), HCV infection (AOR 9.03, 95% CI 1.41-57.76; p = 0.020), Fibrosis-4 (FIB-4) score (AOR 1.45, 95% CI: 1.05-2.34: p < 0.01), and larger tumor size (AOR 1.27, 95% CI 1.11-1.46; p < 0.01) were significantly associated with HCC. Conclusion Ultrasound-guided percutaneous liver biopsy demonstrated a favorable safety profile for the evaluation of FLL. HCC was the predominant histopathologic diagnosis, reflecting the substantial burden of primary liver cancer in this setting. Chronic viral hepatitis and larger tumor size were significantly associated with HCC. These findings support the continued role of US-PLB in the diagnostic evaluation of indeterminate focal liver lesions and underscores the importance of viral hepatitis prevention, surveillance, and early detection strategies in sub-Saharan Africa.

title: Integrating Non-Invasive Liver Assessment into Screening Colonoscopy: A Prospective Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: Introduction Steatotic liver disease is underdiagnosed despite guideline recommendations for risk-based case-finding. Colorectal cancer (CRC) screening colonoscopy engages a prevention-oriented, healthcare-seeking population in whom liver disease may go undetected. We assessed the feasibility, acceptance, and yield of non-invasive liver assessment integrated into screening colonoscopy visits. Methods This prospective cross-sectional study enrolled adults aged ≥50 years attending screening colonoscopy. Individuals with known chronic liver disease were excluded. Participants underwent hepatic ultrasound and point shear wave elastography. Liver stiffness measurements (LSM) were interpreted using prespecified thresholds of 1.30, 1.50, and 1.70 m/s (∼5, 7, and 9 kPa, respectively). We assessed whether risk-factor-based criteria would have identified participants with elevated stiffness, and evaluated the Fibrosis-4 index (FIB-4) against LSM thresholds. Results Of 692 adults offered participation, 610 enrolled (88.2% acceptance); one was excluded for decompensated heart failure. Reliable LSM was obtained in 578 of 609 (94.9%). Ultrasound-defined steatosis was identified in 55.5%. LSM exceeded 1.30 m/s in 25.3%; 9.0% and 5.0% met thresholds consistent with significant fibrosis (≥1.50 m/s) and compensated advanced chronic liver disease (≥1.70 m/s), respectively. Among participants with LSM ≥1.50 m/s, exposure profiles were metabolic in 63.5%, mixed metabolic-alcohol in 21.2%, and alcohol-related in 15.4%. Risk-factor criteria were met by 76.6% and captured 46/52 participants with LSM ≥1.50 m/s. At this threshold, FIB-4 showed modest discrimination (AUROC 0.682); sensitivity decreased from 0.706 using a single threshold to 0.529 using age-adjusted thresholds. Discussion Opportunistic liver assessment integrated into screening colonoscopy was feasible, well accepted, and identified previously undetected steatosis and elevated LSM.

title: Pediatric prolactinoma-associated pituitary apoplexy presenting with acute visual loss: a case report, literature review, and management strategy.
abstract: Objectives Hemorrhagic pituitary apoplexy (PA) in children is exceedingly rare, with approximately 32 cases reported since 1980. Current guidelines recommend cabergoline as first-line therapy; however, acute complete visual loss mandates emergency surgical decompression. No guideline defines the optimal extent of resection, despite gross total resection carrying a 48-54 % risk of panhypopituitarism. Case presentation An 11-year-old prepubertal girl presented with a 2-day history of complete right-eye visual loss. Serum prolactin was 987 μg/L, and MRI demonstrated a hemorrhagic sellar-suprasellar mass compressing the optic chiasm. Emergency endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery was performed with an intentionally limited strategy - hematoma evacuation, optic decompression, and partial debulking - deliberately avoiding aggressive capsular dissection. Histopathology confirmed prolactinoma. Vision was fully restored immediately after extubation, with near-complete visual field recovery on postoperative day 5 (VFI 98 %). Adrenocortical function was preserved. Central hypothyroidism developed, and levothyroxine was initiated. Cabergoline (0.25 mg/week) was started on postoperative day 5, achieving a 93.7 % prolactin reduction by day 20 (987 → 61.9 μg/L). Conclusions In pediatric prolactinoma-associated PA requiring emergency surgery, a decompression-first strategy prioritizing visual rescue and tissue diagnosis over gross total resection may reduce the risk of panhypopituitarism, with residual tumor subsequently managed with cabergoline. The rapid biochemical response documented here supports this approach, though multicenter prospective evaluation is required.

Objectives

Hemorrhagic pituitary apoplexy (PA) in children is exceedingly rare, with approximately 32 cases reported since 1980. Current guidelines recommend cabergoline as first-line therapy; however, acute complete visual loss mandates emergency surgical decompression. No guideline defines the optimal extent of resection, despite gross total resection carrying a 48-54 % risk of panhypopituitarism.

Case presentation

An 11-year-old prepubertal girl presented with a 2-day history of complete right-eye visual loss. Serum prolactin was 987 μg/L, and MRI demonstrated a hemorrhagic sellar-suprasellar mass compressing the optic chiasm. Emergency endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery was performed with an intentionally limited strategy - hematoma evacuation, optic decompression, and partial debulking - deliberately avoiding aggressive capsular dissection. Histopathology confirmed prolactinoma. Vision was fully restored immediately after extubation, with near-complete visual field recovery on postoperative day 5 (VFI 98 %). Adrenocortical function was preserved. Central hypothyroidism developed, and levothyroxine was initiated. Cabergoline (0.25 mg/week) was started on postoperative day 5, achieving a 93.7 % prolactin reduction by day 20 (987 → 61.9 μg/L).

Conclusions

In pediatric prolactinoma-associated PA requiring emergency surgery, a decompression-first strategy prioritizing visual rescue and tissue diagnosis over gross total resection may reduce the risk of panhypopituitarism, with residual tumor subsequently managed with cabergoline. The rapid biochemical response documented here supports this approach, though multicenter prospective evaluation is required.

title: Pulsatile Tinnitus: A Multimodality Imaging Review of Etiology and Diagnostic Evaluation
abstract: Abstract Pulsatile tinnitus is a rhythmic, pulse-synchronous auditory perception that is frequently associated with an underlying vascular or structural abnormality. While tinnitus affects approximately 10–20% of adults, pulsatile tinnitus is relatively uncommon but clinically significant, with an identifiable and potentially treatable cause detected in over 70% of patients and in up to 90% in dedicated imaging cohorts. The etiologic spectrum is broad and includes vascular, structural, systemic, benign, and malignant conditions, some of which may result in serious morbidity if unrecognized. Imaging is central to diagnosis and management, with evaluation commonly performed using high-resolution temporal bone CT, CT angiography and venography, MRI with angiographic and venographic techniques, and digital subtraction angiography in selected cases. This pictorial review integrates multimodality imaging with representative case examples to provide a structured, physiology-based diagnostic approach. By emphasizing key imaging patterns across major etiologic categories, this review aims to enhance diagnostic confidence, streamline imaging workup, and facilitate recognition of actionable causes, thereby supporting timely intervention and improved patient outcomes.

title: Impact of coronary artery calcification detection on cardiovascular care trajectories in patients undergoing lung cancer screening: a systematic review
abstract: Abstract Importance: Coronary artery calcification (CAC) is commonly identified on low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) performed for lung cancer screening (LCS) and is associated with increased cardiovascular (CV) risk. Although guidelines increasingly recommend reporting and incorporating CAC into CV risk stratification, whether its detection translates into downstream CV preventive care remains unclear. Objective: To systematically evaluate reporting practices and downstream clinical management following CAC detection during LDCT LCS. Evidence Review: We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and Web of Science Core Collection from inception to September 23, 2026, and searched grey literature through September 20, 2026. We included original studies of adults undergoing LDCT within established or pilot LCS programs if they evaluated downstream management following CAC detection or reporting. Reviewers independently extracted data in duplicate on CAC assessment, reporting, communication, preventive pharmacotherapy, referrals, investigations, and clinical outcomes. We assessed study quality using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Owing to clinical and methodological heterogeneity, we synthesized findings narratively. Findings: We included twelve studies published between 2020 and 2026 from the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia, and France. Visual assessment was the predominant method for CAC identification, although reporting and communication practices varied substantially. Statin initiation (N=7) ranged from 3% to 38%, cardiology referral (N=3) from 6.9% to 44%, and cardiac stress testing (N=2) from 12.5% to 21.6%. Structured CV follow-up pathways were evaluated in five studies. Three studies found greater a CAC severity or a more explicit reporting was associated with increased statin initiation. Study quality was moderate overall, with NOS scores ranging from four to eight of nine; common limitations included absence of comparator groups and limited adjustment for confounding. Conclusions and Relevance: CAC detected during LCS was followed by variable downstream CV preventive care, and reporting alone does not consistently translate into clinical action. Greater CAC severity and more explicit reporting were associated with increased clinical action in some studies, but reporting alone did not consistently translate into preventive management. Comparative studies are needed to determine whether structured communication and follow-up pathways improve cardiovascular care and clinical outcomes.

title: Striatal tissue iron in depressed and healthy individuals and the effect of buproprion
abstract: Abstract Introduction: Dopaminergic dysfunction in the striatum is thought to play a central role in anhedonia in major depressive disorder (MDD). Normalised T2*-weighted (nT2*w) imaging provides a widely available MRI-derived proxy of striatal tissue iron, an indirect marker of dopaminergic function, but its relationship with reward processing and anhedonia in MDD has not been established. In this secondary analysis, we examined whether striatal nT2*w distinguishes individuals with MDD from healthy controls, is associated with reward learning and clinical symptoms, including anhedonia and depression, and is sensitive to treatment with the dopaminergic antidepressant bupropion Methods Depressed (n = 40) and healthy participants (n = 41) underwent clinical assessment, functional MRI, and a probabilistic instrumental learning task (PILT) at baseline, with follow-up assessments after 2 and 6 weeks. Participants with MDD received open-label bupropion treatment throughout the 6-week study. The primary outcome was MRI-derived striatal tissue iron, quantified using nT2*w signal extracted from resting-state fMRI within the whole striatum, caudate, putamen, and nucleus accumbens. Associations between nT2*w, diagnostic group, reward learning, clinical symptoms, and treatment response were examined. Results At baseline, depressed participants compared to healthy controls showed significantly higher striatal and caudate nT2*w values, indicative of lower tissue iron. The marker demonstrated excellent 2-week test-retest reliability in healthy participants. Striatal nT2*w was not associated with reward learning, anhedonia, or depression severity at baseline, and did not change following 2 weeks of bupropion treatment or predict clinical response after 6 weeks. Across groups, females demonstrated higher nT2*w values (lower tissue iron) than males in the striatum, caudate, and putamen. Discussion Striatal nT2*w represents a promising, robust and widely accessible neuroimaging marker of depression, reliably distinguishing depressed individuals from healthy controls while demonstrating excellent test–retest reliability. Larger longitudinal studies are now needed to establish its clinical utility and determine whether it can detect changes in reward processing and treatment response across the course of illness.

title: Negative Correlation Between ADC Values and GPC3 Expression in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Quantitative Diffusion-Weighted Imaging Study.
abstract: Objective To investigate the association between apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) derived from diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and glypican-3 (GPC3) expression in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), and to explore the potential of ADC as a non-invasive imaging biomarker for assessing GPC3 expression. Methods This retrospective study included 468 patients with pathologically confirmed HCC who underwent preoperative liver magnetic resonance imaging between January 2020 and December 2025. Based on immunohistochemical staining, patients were classified into three groups: GPC3-negative (GPC3-, n=69), low-expression (GPC3+, n=42), and high-expression (GPC3++, n=357). Tumor ADC values, adjacent liver tissue ADC values, and tumor-to-liver ADC ratios were measured and compared among groups. Statistical analyses included the Kruskal-Wallis test, Mann-Whitney U -test with Bonferroni correction, and Spearman correlation analysis. Results Tumor ADC values differed significantly among the three groups (p<0.001), with median ADC values of 1.40 (1.34-1.46), 1.35 (1.28-1.42), and 1.27 (1.23-1.31) ×10 -3 mm 2 /s in the GPC3-, GPC3+, and GPC3++ groups, respectively. The tumor-to-liver ADC ratios were 0.97 (0.94-1.00), 0.91 (0.88-0.94), and 0.87 (0.84-0.90), respectively, and also showed significant differences among groups (p<0.001). ADC values and ADC ratios were negatively correlated with GPC3 expression levels ( r =-0.52 and r =-0.56, respectively; both p<0.001). Conclusion Higher GPC3 expression in HCC was associated with lower tumor ADC values. Quantitative DWI-derived ADC, including both tumor ADC and the tumor-to-liver ADC ratio, may serve as a promising imaging biomarker associated with GPC3 expression, potentially offering supportive information for preoperative evaluation of HCC.

title: Utility of Vorasidenib in IDH1 R132C-Mutant WHO Grade 2 Astrocytoma: A Case Report.
abstract: WHO grade 2 astrocytomas are defined by an IDH mutation and the absence of 1p/19q codeletion. Most harbor the canonical IDH1 R132H substitution; rarer R132X variants, including R132C, remain underrepresented in prospective trials. Vorasidenib, a brain-penetrant dual IDH1/IDH2 inhibitor, prolongs progression-free survival in residual or recurrent grade 2 IDH-mutant glioma and is now included in contemporary North American guidelines when radiotherapy and chemotherapy can be deferred. We report a 25-year-old man who underwent maximal safe resection of a right temporal mass diagnosed as WHO grade 2 astrocytoma, IDH1 R132C mutant, with co-occurring ATRX and TP53 alterations. Serial postoperative MRI showed progressive residual non-enhancing T2/FLAIR signal (7 × 6 mm, then 10×7 mm, then 10×9 mm), and a 2024 biopsy confirmed residual grade 2 tumor without anaplastic features. Vorasidenib 40 mg orally once daily was started in fall 2024. After 17 months of continuous therapy (35 months after resection), the residual non-enhancing focus remains radiographically stable, and no treatment-related adverse events have occurred. Vorasidenib binds an allosteric pocket at the IDH1 dimer interface that does not directly include codon 132, which supports anticipated class activity across R132X variants. This observation is structural, not a demonstration that R132C is more sensitive than R132H. Direct comparative clinical data for R132C remain absent. This case adds real-world evidence that vorasidenib can be used safely in this uncommon molecular subgroup.

title: Improving Postpolypectomy Surveillance Decisions Using an Automated Analysis of Colonoscopy and Histopathology Reports: 2-Center Validation Study.
abstract: Background Postpolypectomy surveillance intervals derived from colonoscopy findings and histopathology should be guideline-based, yet these are frequently not adhered to, contributing to under- and oversurveillance. This motivates a more structured and automated approach to improve adherence. Objective We developed and evaluated an automated, implementable, guideline-aligned decision support tool that extracts colorectal polyp features from free-text colonoscopy and histopathology reports and produces auditable surveillance recommendations. Methods We extracted paired colonoscopy and histopathology reports from a National Health Service (NHS) trust and designed a 4-stage prompting pipeline using open-weight large language models to separate multispecimen histopathology reports into individual containers ("pots"), align endoscopic findings with specimens, and normalize each pot into a structured schema. The surveillance intervals were then computed by a deterministic rule engine encoding guideline rules. We evaluated extraction performance on 100 procedures (215 pots), assessed surveillance recommendation performance on a same-site cohort (n=100), and performed external validation on a cohort from a second trust (n=100). A separate retrospective audit compared automated recommendations and observed routine scheduling against a clinician-derived reference based on full electronic health record review in 127 patients. Results Key extraction fields showed end-to-end accuracy (specimen type=0.995; location=0.981; diagnosis=0.981; excision completeness=0.949), with mean report-level pot comprehensiveness of 0.968 (SD 0.112). Overall surveillance recommendation accuracy was 0.96 (95% CI 0.90-0.98) at Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust (GSTT) and 0.93 (95% CI 0.86-0.97) at Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust (SWB) and showed strong class-level performance (no follow-up F 1 -score of 0.98 at GSTT and 0.97 at SWB; site check F 1 -score of 0.93 at GSTT and 0.91 at SWB; 3-year follow-up F 1 -score of 0.86 at GSTT and 0.80 at SWB; cancer alert F 1 -score of 1.00 at GSTT and 1.00 at SWB). The comparison to current clinical practice showed that the tool would improve guideline adherence primarily by reducing potential undersurveillance. Conclusions This hybrid approach using open-weight large language models for structured extraction and guideline-encoded rules for decision-making can generate accurate, lightweight, and auditable postpolypectomy surveillance recommendations. Such a tool has the potential to improve safety netting and guideline adherence in NHS colonoscopy workflows.

title: AI for Poststroke Epilepsy: Scoping Review of Imaging-Based Prediction Models and Implications for African Settings.
abstract: Background Poststroke seizures (PSS) and poststroke epilepsy (PSE) are important neurological complications associated with poorer functional recovery, increased mortality, and reduced quality of life after stroke. Neuroimaging plays a central role in identifying patients at increased risk, and recent advances in AI have enabled the development of imaging-based prediction models that may improve individualized risk stratification. However, the current evidence remains fragmented, and the extent to which these approaches are applicable to African health care settings is unclear. Objective This scoping review aimed to chart the existing global evidence on the development of imaging-based prediction models that can help in predicting PSS and PSE, especially AI-based ones. The purpose was to look into the imaging techniques, computational algorithms, and validation methodologies used and the representation of African populations. Methods This scoping review was performed using the Joanna Briggs Institute methodological framework, and the results were presented based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) framework. Articles searched using databases such as PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar involved the application of computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), angiography imaging techniques, radiomic markers, or multimodal neuroimaging techniques in statistical and AI-based prediction models for seizure-related outcomes after stroke. Results Twenty-three studies published between 2005 and 2026 met the eligibility criteria. The evidence demonstrated a clear methodological evolution from conventional imaging-based prediction models to radiomics, machine learning, deep learning, explainable AI, and multimodal approaches. MRI and CT were the predominant imaging modalities, with cortical involvement, lesion location, infarct volume, hemorrhagic transformation, and quantitative radiomic features emerging as the most frequently reported imaging predictors. Most AI models relied on internal validation, while relatively few underwent external validation. The evidence base was concentrated in East Asia, Europe, and North America, with no eligible imaging-based AI models having been developed or externally validated using African datasets. Conclusions Imaging-based AI for predicting PSS and PSE has progressed rapidly, but important methodological and geographical gaps remain. Limited external validation, heterogeneous reporting, and the absence of African development and validation cohorts restrict confidence in the generalizability of existing models. Future research should prioritize the development of explainable imaging-based AI models using representative African neuroimaging datasets and their external validation in multicenter studies.

title: Metastasis Extraction From Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Clinical Notes Using Large Language Model-Based Classification: Retrospective Comparative Study.
abstract: Background Identification of metastasis status in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a critical part of understanding disease prognosis, treatment courses, trial eligibility, and population-level cancer surveillance. However, metastasis status is inconsistently recorded in structured cancer registry fields, since manual abstraction of clinical notes is often an error-prone process. This challenge highlights an opportunity for leveraging large language models (LLMs) to conduct high-scale metastasis extraction from real-world clinical documentation. Objective We conducted a retrospective, multicohort comparative evaluation of 3 distinct LLMs for 2 independent classification tasks: overall metastasis presence at any site and brain/central nervous system (CNS) metastasis presence. We evaluated model performance on 2 independent NSCLC cohorts: one with registry labels and another with manual annotations. We further explored whether our methods could analyze clinical documentation and recover missing information in structured registry fields. Methods Patient cohorts were derived from the Winship Cancer Institute. Cohort 1 (n=579 patients; 24,887 notes across 69 note types; 2023-2025) used registry-linked metastasis fields as the reference standard. Cohort 2 (n=22 patients; 644 radiology notes; 2010-2021) was drawn from 2 completed randomized trials and used dual-annotated labels (Cohen κ: 0.93 overall metastasis; 0.88 CNS metastasis) as the reference standard. We fine-tuned the GatorTron-base encoder model for each independent binary classification task. We evaluated MedGemma-27B-text and Llama 3.1-70B using zero-shot prompting. A separate cohort of 675 patients with missing registry labels was used for an exploratory missingness-recovery analysis, validated against annotations of a random subsample. Our best-performing model was used to conduct further site-specific metastasis classification, based on available registry data. Results More than half (675/1260, 54%) of initially identified cohort 1 patients had missing or unknown registry metastasis labels. MedGemma demonstrated the best performance in overall metastasis classification (cohort 1: F 1 -score=0.80; cohort 2 patient-level: F 1 -score=1.0; cohort 2 note-level: F 1 -score=0.93). For brain/CNS metastasis, Llama3 performed best in both cohorts (cohort 1: F 1 -score=0.79; cohort 2 patient-level: F 1 -score=0.93; cohort 2 note-level: F 1 -score=0.86). The fine-tuned GatorTron model showed strong performance for classification of overall metastasis in cohort 1 (F 1 -score=0.72). Error analysis indicated that several model errors reflected incomplete registry labels, ambiguous clinical language, or missing documentation. In the exploratory recovery analysis, model predictions agreed with manual annotations at an accuracy of 0.90 and F 1 -score of 0.89. Additional site-specific metastasis classification by MedGemma demonstrated high performance for liver metastasis (F 1 -score=0.82) and bone metastasis (F 1 -score=0.79). Conclusions All models demonstrated relatively high performance. The zero-shot generative models were more robust to nuanced documentation and context-dependent brain/CNS metastasis extraction. The fine-tuned encoder model demonstrated strong classification performance but may have been limited by potential inaccuracies in the registry reference standards during model training. This study further demonstrated the potential of LLMs in recovering plausible structured labels from narrative text, complementing cancer registries for metastasis ascertainment.

title: Survival disparities in primary malignant spine tumors: a national analysis of academic and community hospital care.
abstract: Objective Primary malignant osseous tumors of the mobile spine are rare and require complex, multidisciplinary care. Treatment outcomes may differ between academic and community hospitals due to variations in resources, expertise, and infrastructure. This study evaluates demographics, care delivery patterns, and clinical outcomes, including both short- and long-term survival, for patients treated at academic versus community cancer programs using the National Cancer Database. Methods A retrospective analysis of a prospectively maintained database was performed. Nine hundred forty-three patients diagnosed with primary malignant osseous tumors of the mobile spine between 2004 and 2017 were identified. Patients were stratified by facility type: there were 601 patients treated at academic comprehensive cancer programs (ACADs) and 342 treated at comprehensive community cancer programs (CCCPs). Demographic, treatment, and clinical data were compared using descriptive statistics. Outcomes included inpatient length of stay, time to treatment, 30- and 90-day mortality, vital status at last contact, and overall survival. A multivariable Cox proportional hazards model assessed factors associated with overall survival. Results Patients at ACADs were significantly younger and more likely to have private insurance. The size and histopathological composition of the tumors did not differ significantly between facility types. ACAD patients experienced significantly longer inpatient stays and longer time to radiation initiation among patients receiving radiation with documented start dates. Time to chemotherapy did not significantly differ (p = 0.91). Thirty- and 90-day mortality were comparable between facility types among eligible surgical cases. At last follow-up, a significantly greater proportion of ACAD patients were alive (50.2% vs 38.3%, p < 0.001), and the median time from diagnosis to last contact or death was longer at ACADs (40.8 vs 33.2 months, p = 0.001). In the primary multivariable Cox model, treatment at an academic facility was associated with improved overall survival (hazard ratio [HR] 0.766, 95% CI 0.627-0.937; p = 0.009). In a sensitivity model adjusting for histopathology rather than grade, this association was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (CCCP vs ACAD, HR 1.19, p = 0.081). Conclusions Patients treated at academic centers had longer inpatient stays and longer time to radiation initiation, yet academic facility treatment was associated with improved overall survival in the primary multivariable model. After accounting for histopathological subtype in sensitivity analysis, the facility-type association was attenuated, suggesting survival differences reflect both tumor biology and system-level care pathways.
