title: Spatial localization patterns in MRI-negative Cushing disease: a comparative pituitary heat map analysis.
abstract: Objective MRI-negative Cushing disease is challenging to treat due to difficulty with tumor localization and lower biochemical remission rates. Surgeons primarily rely on visual and tactile feedback to identify abnormal pituitary tissue. In this study, the authors analyzed intraoperative sketches of histology-confirmed corticotroph adenomas to compare the spatial distributions of MRI-positive and MRI-negative tumors. By characterizing these distribution patterns, the authors aimed to improve the localization and surgical targeting of MRI-negative pathology. Methods The authors retrospectively reviewed patients with Cushing disease who underwent microscopic transsphenoidal resection by the late Dr. Edward H. Oldfield at the authors' institution from December 2007 to March 2017. Patients were stratified into MRI-positive and MRI-negative cohorts. A standardized pituitary sketch visualizing both coronal and sagittal planes was used for postoperative documentation. For every patient, Dr. Oldfield annotated the anatomical location of the histologically confirmed corticotroph adenoma. Image acquisition, processing, and heat map-based spatial analysis were performed to assess cumulative tumor density. Spatial differences were evaluated with cluster-based correction for multiple comparisons. Surgical outcomes were then compared between the 2 cohorts. Results A total of 153 patients with Cushing disease and histologically confirmed pituitary corticotroph adenoma (133 MRI-positive and 20 MRI-negative adenomas) were analyzed. Baseline demographic and biochemical characteristics were similar across MRI status. Both cohorts demonstrated similar anatomical presentation, with over 50% of patients presenting with corticotroph adenomas in the anterior aspect of the pituitary gland. MRI-positive tumors were more likely to localize to the lateral and dorsal aspects of the anterior pituitary (p < 0.05). In contrast, MRI-negative adenomas showed no distinct area of increased prevalence. Postoperatively, the MRI-negative cohort had higher nadir cortisol levels (2.9 vs 1.5 μg/dl, p = 0.001) and increased reoperation rates (20% vs 3.8%, p = 0.027). Remission rates were lower in MRI-negative patients but not statistically significant (75.0% vs 91.0%, p = 0.050). Conclusions MRI-negative corticotroph adenomas were less frequently localized in the lateral and dorsal aspects of the anterior pituitary compared to MRI-positive tumors, with no distinct region of increased prevalence. These findings support a unique surgical strategy that leverages the anatomical distribution of histologically confirmed adenomas to guide gland exploration and resection of hidden tumors. While these observations may provide anatomical context for surgical exploration in radiographically occult disease, operative decision-making should remain guided by intraoperative findings and individual patient anatomy.

title: Quantitative MRI to assess baseline shunt flow in patients with hydrocephalus: a noninvasive tool to aid clinical decision-making.
abstract: Objective Hydrocephalus is a common yet serious condition, and ventricular shunts are used for lifesaving CSF diversion. Existing methods for shunt evaluation provide correlative/qualitative information, leading to commonplace clinical diagnostic challenges. The aim of this study was to determine accurate and noninvasive measures of volumetric CSF flow rates through ventricular shunts using the phase-contrast (PC) sequence in routine MRI for pediatric patients with hydrocephalus. Methods The authors conducted a prospective observational cohort study of patients with ventricular shunts who underwent a clinically indicated brain MRI and the adjunct PC-MRI shunt flow sequence at a single center between January 2023 and January 2024. At the study institution, PC-MRI has been integrated as a supplementary imaging technique to quantify shunt flow alongside fast protocol MRI for shunted patients. Clinical and imaging data were collected. Data distributions and paired changes in flow measurements over time were assessed using appropriate statistical tests. Results Overall, 207 patients (107 male, mean age 11.3 years [range 8 days-27 years]) who underwent PC-MRI were included; 98% had a VP shunt. The mean CSF flow rate was 9.9 ± 8 mL/hour (range 0.5-54 mL/hour). No significant differences were noted by age, sex, etiology of hydrocephalus, valve type, time interval since shunt placement, BMI, fronto-occipital horn ratio, and frontal horn or atrial width. Repeat PC-MRI was performed in 11 patients, and there was no significant difference in flow measurements between initial and follow-up images (p = 0.83) among these patients. PC-MRI identified alterations that accurately demonstrated failure in 3 patients and avoided unnecessary surgery in a fourth patient. Conclusions Addition of PC-MRI to routine imaging examinations in patients with ventricular shunts accurately and noninvasively measured CSF shunt flow. Flow rate data can provide supplementary information regarding shunt function and serve as a baseline for future comparison assessments. These findings suggest a role for routine acquisition of patient-specific baseline shunt flow measurement in shunted pediatric patients with hydrocephalus.

title: Mixed Pneumonia with Pulmonary Embolism and Multiple Pathogens Detected in Bronchoalveolar Lavage Fluid: A Case Report.
abstract: Severe community-acquired pneumonia may involve mixed pathogens and concurrent vascular complications. A 72-year-old man presented with fever, nonproductive cough, vomiting, hypoxemia, markedly elevated inflammatory markers, and an elevated D-dimer concentration. Chest computed tomography showed left lower-lobe consolidation and pleural effusion. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography, obtained because of hypoxemia and suspected pulmonary embolism, showed a filling defect in a right upper-lobe pulmonary artery. The patient received antimicrobial therapy prior to bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL). Bronchoscopy was performed in the bronchopulmonary segment corresponding to the radiographic lesion, and approximately 10 mL of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) was recovered aseptically for microbiological and cytological testing. An aliquot of at least 3 mL was allocated to a multiplex pathogen-targeted sequencing assay, which detected Chlamydia psittaci, influenza A H3N2, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and additional conditionally pathogenic or commensal organisms. The three principal detections were interpreted in conjunction with the clinical presentation, imaging, inflammatory markers, BALF cytology, conventional testing, and treatment response. The patient improved during antimicrobial and anticoagulant treatment and was discharged on December 3, 2025. At the documented outpatient follow-up on December 17, rivaroxaban was continued for approximately one further month. This case highlights the adjunctive value and interpretive limitations of targeted sequencing in a treated patient. The serial imaging and invasive sampling reflected case-specific decisions and should not be interpreted as a routine protocol for pneumonia.

title: A Standardized Workflow for Multimodal Assessment of Right-to-Left Shunt-Related Ischemic Brain Injury.
abstract: Right-to-left shunt (RLS) has been associated with cryptogenic stroke, migraine, and other neurological conditions in which ischemic brain injury may be clinically relevant. In routine practice, however, assessment is often fragmented. Shunt presence may be documented, but shunt burden, provoked versus non-provoked patterns, anatomical complexity, and MRI-defined brain injury are not always integrated into a reproducible workflow. Here, we describe a standardized protocol for multimodal assessment of RLS-related ischemic brain injury in a clinically selected cohort. The workflow includes patient screening, exclusion of major vascular and systemic factors that could independently contribute to brain parenchymal injury, contrast-enhanced transcranial Doppler ultrasound (c-TCD) confirmation and shunt grading, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) classification, transthoracic and/or transesophageal echocardiographic anatomical assessment, structured data extraction, and dataset cleaning. To improve reproducibility, the protocol also standardizes key coding steps, including shunt-grade harmonization, classification of RLS as simple or complex, and interpretation of D-dimer values reported below the assay threshold. Using this workflow, a harmonized analytic cohort of 60 RLS-positive patients was established. MRI identified 23 MRI-negative and 37 MRI-positive patients. Representative analyses showed that MRI-positive findings were more frequent in patients with greater shunt burden and more complex anatomical phenotypes. This protocol provides an operational model for incorporating c-TCD, MRI, echocardiography, and structured clinical parameters into the evaluation of MRI-defined ischemic brain injury in RLS-positive patients. It should be interpreted as a workflow for standardized multimodal phenotyping rather than as a standalone physiologic assessment of all clinically significant or hypoxemia-related RLS.

title: HeartFusion: A Cross-Modality Transformer for Accurate Cardiovascular Disease Diagnosis and Severity Assessment.
abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) requires diagnostic models that can integrate complementary electrophysiological and anatomical information while also representing ordered disease severity. HeartFusion was developed as a mathematically informed cross-modality Transformer framework combining electrocardiogram (ECG) and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Wavelet-derived ECG time-frequency representations were encoded with Cardioformer, MRI structure was encoded with TransUNet, and modality-specific embeddings were aligned in a shared latent space using cosine-similarity-based cross-modal attention. A transformer classifier performed diagnostic prediction, while an ordinal regression head modeled four ordered severity stages. Three controlled pseudo-paired benchmark cohorts were constructed from PTB-XL with ACDC (CVD-I), MIMIC-IV-ECG with CMRxRecon (CVD-II), and PTB-XL/MIMIC-IV-ECG with OCMR/Cardiac Atlas Project data (CVD-III). Source observations were partitioned before pseudo-pair construction to prevent cross-partition leakage, and five matched random seeds were used for evaluation. HeartFusion achieved diagnostic accuracies of 97.73%, 98.23%, and 98.02%, with AUC values of 98.12%, 98.76%, and 98.39% on CVD-I, CVD-II, and CVD-III, respectively. Severity staging achieved ordinal accuracies above 90%, with the best Cohen's kappa of 0.839 and MAE of 0.340. These findings support phenotype-level multimodal representation learning, while validation on genuinely patient-matched ECG-MRI cohorts remains necessary before clinical deployment.

title: Experimental Protocols for Developing and Validating Explainable AI Models in Secure Healthcare Diagnostics.
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has drastically enhanced healthcare diagnostics with automated disease detection, predictive analytics, and intelligent systems for clinical decision support. Nevertheless, the black-box nature of deep learning models hampers interpretability, clinical trust, and regulatory acceptance and raises concerns about data privacy and cybersecurity. This paper presents comprehensive experimental frameworks for developing and evaluating explainable AI models for secure healthcare diagnostics. The suggested model combines responsible data management, multimodal preprocessing, secure deep learning models, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods, and reproducible validation procedures in a single healthcare diagnostic pipeline. Methods of explaining, such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, and counterfactual analysis, were used to make the models more transparent and understandable for clinicians. At the same time, federated learning and differential privacy methods were used to securely manage highly sensitive patient data. Experimental evaluation has shown 96% classification accuracy, 94% sensitivity, and 95% specificity. These results were consistent in heterogeneous healthcare datasets. Compared to traditional black-box models, the explainability framework not only enhanced the interpretability of the results but also more accurately identified the regions relevant for diagnosis. Moreover, the secure federated learning architecture minimized privacy leakages without sacrificing the predictive performance and remained robust even when exposed to adversarial perturbations. An external evaluation also confirmed the reproducibility and generalizability of the protocols involved. This methodology offers a comprehensive and reliable foundation for deploying AI-powered diagnostics across multiple healthcare domains: radiology, pathology, oncology, cardiology, neurology, and precision medicine.

title: Clinical Application of Three-dimensional Laparoscopic Artery-first Pancreaticoduodenectomy in Treating Pancreatic Head Malignant Tumors.
abstract: Pancreaticoduodenectomy is a technically demanding procedure associated with substantial surgical risk. Conventional laparoscopic approaches have several limitations, including restricted visualization, which can make exposure of the superior mesenteric artery and identification of vessels and lymph nodes challenging. In patients with vascular adhesion or tumor invasion, surgical dissection is particularly difficult and may increase the risk of intraoperative vascular injury and hemorrhage. In addition, poor delineation of anatomical planes may result in incomplete tumor dissection, inadequate lymphadenectomy, and difficult mobilization of the pancreatic head and duodenum, potentially compromising surgical safety and oncological outcomes. To optimize the surgical workflow, this protocol describes a three-dimensional laparoscopic artery-first pancreaticoduodenectomy with the infracolic artery-first approach as the principal technical modification. By combining early arterial exposure and clear delineation of anatomical planes with the stereoscopic visualization of three-dimensional laparoscopy, this technique facilitates identification of vessel-tissue relationships, vascular control, lymphadenectomy, tumor dissection, and tissue mobilization. These features may help reduce inadvertent vascular injury and intraoperative blood loss while enabling complete tumor resection. The protocol provides a standardized surgical approach, particularly applicable to pancreatic head lesions adjacent to or involving major vessels, and is intended to improve the safety and reproducibility of laparoscopic pancreaticoduodenectomy.

title: Structural Evaluation of Retinal and Choroidal Features in Eyes With Primary Microtropia.
abstract: Purpose To investigate the structural characteristics of the macula, optic nerve head, and choroid in eyes with primary microtropia using spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT). Methods This prospective case-control study included 50 pediatric patients with a diagnosis of primary microtropia. Each participant contributed data from both eyes. Eyes were categorized as microtropic, fellow, or healthy control. All patients underwent comprehensive ophthalmic evaluation, including SD-OCT imaging. Parameters assessed included central macular thickness, total macular volume, regional retinal thickness, peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer thickness, subfoveal and regional choroidal thickness, and choroidal vascular index. Results No statistically significant differences were observed among microtropic, fellow, and control eyes in terms of central macular thickness, total macular volume, or peripapillary retinal nerve fiber layer thickness ( P > .05). Although microtropic eyes showed a mild trend toward increased parafoveal and perifoveal retinal thickness across all quadrants, this variation did not reach statistical significance. Similarly, subfoveal, nasal, and temporal choroidal thickness measurements, as well as choroidal vascularity index, luminal area, stromal area, and total choroidal area, were comparable across all groups. Conclusions Primary microtropia was not associated with measurable retinal or choroidal structural abnormalities on SD-OCT. Although reduced visual acuity was present, the lack of detectable anatomical changes warrants further investigation to determine whether functional impairment in microtropia occurs independently of structural alterations.

title: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada disease misdiagnosed as angle closure: Demographic characteristics, clinical presentation, and visual outcomes.
abstract: Purpose To describe the clinical presentation, diagnostic delay, management, and visual outcomes of Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) disease presenting initially as angle closure. Methods This retrospective study reviewed the medical records of patients diagnosed with VKH who initially presented with angle closure between January 2013 and December 2020. Clinical features, intraocular pressure (IOP), imaging, treatment modalities, and final visual outcomes were analyzed. Univariate and multivariate analyses were performed to identify factors influencing final BCVA (best corrected visual acuity). Results Among 768 VKH patients, 18 patients (36 eyes; 3.94%) presented with angle closure with a mean age of 44.4 years and a female preponderance (89%). Eighteen eyes had primary angle closure (PAC), and 18 eyes had secondary angle closure glaucoma (SACG) at presentation. The mean IOP at final follow-up decreased from 26.3 to 14 mmHg. Fundus evaluation was deferred in many due to media opacities, leading to delayed VKH diagnosis (median delay: 1 month to 7 years). Ancillary imaging revealed choroidal thickening and ciliochoroidal effusion in four eyes. Poorer presenting BCVA and delayed diagnosis (>1 month) were associated with worse final BCVA ( P = 0.011 and P = 0.0066, respectively) in univariate analysis, while presenting BCVA remained a statistically significant independent predictor of final visual outcome (p 0.039) in multivariate analysis. Conclusion VKH can uncommonly present as angle closure, often mimicking PAC or SACG. Early clinical suspicion, use of posterior segment imaging (optical coherence tomography, B-scan, ultrasound biomicroscopy), and prompt immunosuppressive therapy are essential for optimal management.

title: Dual-energy computed tomography pulmonary angiography for pulmonary embolism: a three-tier evidence framework to guide individualized low-iodine scanning.
abstract: Dual-energy computed tomography (DECT) pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is widely studied for pulmonary embolism (PE) evaluation, but heterogeneity in protocols, platforms, and study designs complicates its clinical positioning. This narrative review, with structured search elements adapted from the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020, synthesized evidence from PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (January 2016-June 2026); 28 studies were eligible (26 of 1,287 screened records and 2 identified through citation tracing). Evidence was organized into a three-tier framework (image quality, diagnostic performance, and clinical outcomes). Low-keV virtual monoenergetic imaging at 40-50 keV improves vascular attenuation and enables iodine load reduction to approximately 6 g in selected protocols. Pooled meta-analytic evidence shows no consistent diagnostic advantage of DECT over single-energy CT. The right ventricular/left ventricular diameter ratio remains the most stable prognostic indicator; DECT perfusion metrics have not surpassed it for mortality prediction. Iodine-map hypoperfusion in distal arteries is suspicious for, but not morphologically confirmed as, subsegmental PE; such findings carry a risk of overdiagnosis and warrant caution before anticoagulation. title: Pixel-Level Quantification of Subcutaneous Shear-Wave Velocity Heterogeneity for Grading Lymphatic Obstruction in Breast Cancer-Related Lymphedema
abstract: ObjectivesTo develop and validate pixel data analysis (PDA) for reconstructing pixel-level shear-wave velocity (SWV) from saved Holder-Optimized Elastography (HOE) elastograms and to determine whether whole-field subcutaneous heterogeneity provides a quantitative signature of lymphatic obstruction compared with visual high-velocity-area (HVA) counting and sparse manual region-of-interest (ROI) sampling. Materials and MethodsIn this cross-sectional study, 110 women after breast cancer surgery underwent lymphoscintigraphy and HOE, a pressure-minimized acquisition framework that preserves conventionally captured SWV information while additionally revealing spatial abnormalities attenuated by handheld acquisition. Reconstruction validation used 200 paired ROIs, spanning nearly the full displayed SWV range, from 49 images retrieved from the picture archiving and communication system; reproducibility was assessed across 96 matched anatomical sites from 6 participants undergoing independently reacquired HOE examinations. PDA, visual HVA counting, and manual ROI sampling were evaluated on the same HOE-acquired elastograms in task-specific common complete-case cohorts. ResultsPDA reconstructed the machine-reported SWV with near-zero error over a range of 1.17 - 9.97 m/s (mean difference, +0.0009 m/s; mean absolute error, 0.0075 m/s; 95% limits of agreement, -0.0202 to +0.0221 m/s). For subcutaneous variance, interobserver/intraobserver intraclass correlation coefficients were 0.709/0.799 for PDA and 0.178/0.560 for manual ROI sampling. In the primary no obstruction versus partial obstruction comparison (n = 93), forearm-pooled PDA subcutaneous variance ratio yielded the highest observed area under the curve (AUC, 0.858; 95% confidence interval, 0.771 - 0.946), compared with 0.820 for visual HVA counting and 0.794 for manual ROI sampling. PDAs subcutaneous variance ratio remained a leading feature across all three comparisons (AUC, 0.858 - 0.878), including partial versus total obstruction grading, where all three frameworks showed high discrimination. ConclusionsPDA accurately reconstructs pixel-level SWV from saved HOE elastograms and enables reproducible whole-field quantification of superficial shear-wave elastography heterogeneity. Subcutaneous variance ratio was the leading quantitative PDA feature across lymphatic-obstruction comparisons and was particularly informative in partial obstruction. The same approach also enables retrospective quantitative reanalysis of compatible archived elastograms. Plain-Language SummaryPixel data analysis (PDA) reconstructs quantitative pixel-level shear-wave velocity from saved superficial elastography images, allowing the complete measurable color field to be analyzed rather than a few manually sampled regions. Reconstructed values closely matched machine measurements, and whole-field subcutaneous variance was substantially more reproducible than manual ROI sampling. Subcutaneous variance ratio remained a leading diagnostic signal across obstruction severities, including in partial obstruction without visually detectable high-velocity areas.

title: A defined multi-kingdom microbial consortium naturalizes the immune system of laboratory mice
abstract: Dirty mice experiments suggest that laboratory mice fail to model certain human immune responses due to their limited microbial exposure. The identity, nature, and number of microbes required to normalize the immune system are unknown. Through systematic screening, we uncovered unexpected cross-kingdom microbial interactions and identified four enteric microbes spanning viruses, fungi, and protists sufficient to reproduce key immunological features of pet store mice and adult humans. This consortium also altered cancer outcomes, shifting tumorigenesis toward the anatomical pattern of human familial adenomatous polyposis in ApcMin/+ mice and recapitulating the imperfect response of many patients to chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy. Thus, surprisingly few microbes can profoundly reshape immune states and disease responses, providing a tractable approach to naturalize laboratory mouse immunity.

title: Childhood Trauma and Cortical Thickness in Bipolar Disorder with and without Psychosis: Effects by Diagnostic Group and Trauma Subtype
abstract: Abstract Background Bipolar disorder affects about 2-3% of the population and is associated with cortical abnormalities, with bipolar disorder with psychosis (BDP) reported to show more pronounced changes. It remains unclear whether childhood trauma is associated with cortical thickness differences across bipolar disorder subgroups, particularly in BDP. Methods Using the publicly available PARDIP (Psychosis and Affective Research Domains and Intermediate Phenotypes) data set, we examined whether childhood trauma was associated with cortical thickness differences among 120 individuals: 33 with bipolar disorder without psychosis (BD; 36% male), 38 with bipolar disorder with psychosis (BDP; 47% male), and 49 healthy controls (HC; 61% male). Participants completed the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire-Short Form (CTQ-SF), and T1-weighted MRI scans were processed with FreeSurfer to extract cortical thickness across the 68 Desikan-Killiany regions. Linear mixed effects models tested associations between CTQ subtype scores and cortical thickness and trauma-by-diagnosis interactions, with sensitivity analyses for medication class and illness duration following the ENIGMA guidelines. Results No cortical thickness difference survived correction for multiple testing. At the nominal level, BD showed reduced thickness relative to HC in cingulate, frontal and occipital regions, whereas BDP showed greater superior temporal thickness relative to BD. Sexual abuse was nominally associated with reduced temporal thickness. Exploratory trauma-by-diagnosis interactions suggested region- and subtype-specific patterns that did not survive correction. Medication class and illness duration showed no significant effects after FDR correction. Conclusions These exploratory findings suggest nominal, region-specific associations between childhood trauma subtypes and cortical thickness in bipolar disorder. However, no findings survived correction for multiple comparisons, so they should be read as preliminary and need replication in larger samples.

title: Facilitating Valid Statistical Inference in Biomedical Image Synthesis
abstract: Generative AI for medical image synthesis is increasingly used to impute missing data and augment biomedical datasets. Yet despite achieving high computational similarity to their real-world counterparts, synthetic images remain uncommon in clinical research practice, in part because of concerns about their biological validity. Here, we evaluate whether synthetic images support reliable downstream statistical analysis and biological inference in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and multiplexed immunofluorescence (mIF) imaging. We find that associations between patient phenotypes and synthesized images can be severely attenuated. This is because synthesis methods typically omit clinically relevant covariates and therefore generate images that, although visually realistic, mask key biological differences. Furthermore, naive analyses treat synthesized images as if they were observed, ignoring the statistical uncertainty introduced by synthesis. Drawing on multiple imputation theory, we introduce Phenotype Aware Multiple Synthesis (PAMS), an analysis framework that requires no model retraining and instead adjusts synthesized output to recover valid biological estimates with appropriately calibrated uncertainty. Applied to MRI and mIF data, PAMS reduced estimation bias and restored nominal confidence interval coverage. Because it is compatible with existing synthesis pipelines, PAMS offers a practical and rigorous route to statistically and biologically valid use of synthesized images in biomedical imaging research.

title: Understanding Performance Plateaus and Representation Collapse in 3D MRI Transformers Trained to Classify Brain Disease
abstract: In medical imaging AI, we commonly assume that diagnostic classifiers will increase in accuracy if they are trained on more data, but in reality, their performance often plateaus. To understand this behavior, we ran a spectral analysis of 3D vision transformers, a common supervised deep learning model that can be trained to classify disease based on 3D brain MRI. For simpler classification methods such as linear discriminant analysis, the classifier performance AUC(N), when trained on a sample of size N, is known to depend on the encoder′s eigenspectrum. Each class-discriminative direction in the latent space contributes only after the sample size N reaches a threshold, so the spectrum influences how performance scales with training data. Building on this theory, we show that supervised transformers compress almost all of their discriminative signal into one principal component (EVR@1 = 0.90—0.96): after this representation collapse happens, no further directions cross the threshold as training data increases, and accuracy plateaus. In principle, this plateau in performance could be due to either the encoder′s learned feature space or the difficulty of the task. To distinguish these cases, we trained three types of supervised 3D transformers (ViT3D, MINiT, NIT) and, as a non-collapsing alternative, a frozen self-supervised encoder (DINO), to classify people with dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) versus cognitively normal (CN) individuals from 3D brain MRI, using data from the Alzheimer′s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). We froze each encoder and applied it to a new task, so that only the task difficulty varied. An easy task encoder (Dementia vs CN), transferred to the harder task (MCI vs CN), did not reproduce the plateau (MINiT threshold 9.2), but full retraining did (2758.5). The plateau is therefore due to the learned encoder, rather than task difficulty. Ranking the feature directions by the proportion of the disease signal they contain, we were able to identify a sign of representation collapse, i.e., a single dominant spike in the latent feature eigenspectrum. This spike was 11—26 times larger than predicted from the rest of the spectrum for the disease-trained (supervised) encoders, but was absent for DINO (0.66). To predict how transformer accuracy scales with the number of training scans, a large spike in the encoder spectrum suggests that the representation has collapsed and additional scans will not help; a small spike means that the signal is spread across many encoder latent space directions, and more training data should boost the classifier performance.

title: Hepatic Metastasis of Meningioma Treated with Partial Hepatectomy: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Meningioma is one of the most common central nervous system tumors; however, metastatic lesions are extremely rare. Particularly, hepatic metastasis from meningioma is uncommon, and its diagnosis and optimal management remain undefined. Case presentation A 70-year-old man with a history of left parietal meningioma resection in 2011 and gamma knife therapy for recurrence in the left lateral ventricle in June 2025. A PET-CT scan performed for cancer screening in June 2025 revealed abnormal fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in segment 8 of the liver, with a maximum standardized uptake value of 6.2. CT, and MRI revealed multiple hepatic masses. All tumor markers were within normal ranges. A percutaneous liver biopsy indicated a spindle cell tumor; however, the diagnosis remained inconclusive. For diagnostic and therapeutic purposes, partial hepatectomy of segments 6 and 8 and cholecystectomy were performed. Histopathological examination revealed proliferating spindle-shaped tumor cells arranged in fascicles. Immunohistochemical staining was positive for vimentin, epithelial membrane antigen, and somatostatin receptor 2, confirming the diagnosis of hepatic metastasis from meningioma. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient was discharged in good condition. Conclusions Hepatic metastasis from meningioma is extremely rare; however, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of hepatic tumors in patients with a history of meningioma. Surgical resection is valuable in establishing a definitive diagnosis and achieving local disease control.

title: Small Bowel Volvulus Diagnosed and Treated Using Intraoperative Angiography in a Hybrid Operating Room: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Small bowel volvulus is a surgical emergency that may cause mesenteric ischemia; however, diagnosis may be difficult when bowel perfusion appears preserved. Case presentation An 84-year-old man presented with recurrent postprandial abdominal pain and melena 6 months after a total pharyngolaryngectomy with a jejunal free flap reconstruction. Extensive endoscopic evaluations, including capsule endoscopy, revealed no bleeding source. Contrast-enhanced CT revealed the whirl sign at the root of the small-bowel mesentery with the narrowing of the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), while bowel wall enhancement was preserved. Because the symptoms recurred after resuming oral intake, a hybrid surgery combined with angiography was planned for both diagnostic and therapeutic purposes. The SMA angiography demonstrated significant stenosis without apparent bowel hypoperfusion. After the intra-arterial administration of alprostadil, distal mesenteric perfusion deteriorated on the angiography, and laparoscopic exploration revealed ischemic changes consistent with small bowel volvulus. Because laparoscopic reduction was difficult, an open reduction was performed. Repeat angiography confirmed the resolution of the SMA narrowing and the restoration of distal flow. The patient's symptoms resolved completely. Conclusions The hybrid surgery enabled a functional assessment of mesenteric hemodynamics and immediate surgical treatment during a single procedure. It may be useful in selected patients with small bowel volvulus who have preserved bowel perfusion at rest but recurrent symptoms suggestive of intermittent mesenteric ischemia, and in whom the indication for surgical detorsion remains uncertain.

title: Pancreaticoduodenectomy after Laparoscopic Sleeve Gastrectomy with Preservation of Gastric Arterial Inflow: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Obesity is an established risk factor for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. As laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) has become increasingly prevalent, pancreatic surgeons may encounter malignancies in patients with a surgically altered gastric anatomy. Pancreaticoduodenectomy (PD) after an LSG is rare and requires meticulous preoperative planning to prevent ischemic and anastomotic complications. Case presentation A 47-year-old man with morbid obesity (BMI 59.1 kg/m 2 ) underwent LSG. Twenty-three days later, obstructive jaundice led to the diagnosis of pancreatic head adenocarcinoma. After neoadjuvant chemotherapy and substantial weight reduction (BMI 34.9 kg/m 2 ), subtotal stomach-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy with wedge resection of the superior mesenteric vein was performed. Preoperative CT confirmed the preservation and patency of both the left and right gastric arteries. The left gastric artery was preserved intraoperatively. Gastrojejunostomy was performed using a hand-sewn anastomosis between the greater curvature side of the sleeve stomach and the jejunum. The patient developed a grade B postoperative pancreatic fistula but was discharged with no ischemic complications. Conclusions PD after an LSG is feasible, but careful vascular assessment, a preplanned reconstruction strategy, consideration of the patient's metabolic and nutritional status, and careful intraoperative assessment of the remnant stomach may enhance surgical safety.

title: Impact of FOSL1 polymorphisms and expression on disease progression in oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma.
abstract: Oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (OTSCC) is the most common subtype of oral cancer, with betel quid chewing, tobacco smoking, and alcohol consumption recognized as major risk factors. This study investigated the associations between FOSL1 single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and disease susceptibility and clinicopathological characteristics in OTSCC patients. Three FOSL1 SNPs (rs637571, rs653914, and rs10896065) were genotyped in 377 male OTSCC patients and 1,194 controls using real-time polymerase chain reaction. The FOSL1 rs10896065 polymorphic T variant was significantly associated with advanced clinical stage (Stage III-IV; AOR = 1.663, 95% CI = 1.059-2.611, p = 0.027) and larger tumor size (AOR = 1.813, 95% CI = 1.162-2.831, p = 0.009). Among betel quid chewers, carriers of the CT+TT genotype showed significant associations with advanced clinical stage, larger tumor size, and moderate-to-poor tumor differentiation. Similar associations with advanced stage and greater tumor size were observed among smokers carrying the CT+TT genotype. Analysis of The Cancer Genome Atlas dataset further demonstrated that elevated FOSL1 mRNA expression was significantly associated with larger tumor size (T3-T4 vs. T1-T2, p = 0.0216). These findings suggest that the FOSL1 rs10896065 T allele is associated with advanced clinicopathological features in OTSCC patients, particularly among betel-quid chewers and smokers. FOSL1 polymorphisms may have potential as biomarkers associated with clinicopathological characteristics in OTSCC.

title: L2GSSL: Label-Efficient Local-to-Global Self-Supervised Learning for Volumetric Healthcare Data
abstract: Healthcare institutions routinely accumulate high-dimensional computed tomography (CT) volumes, but only a fraction can be annotated by experts. We present L2GSSL, a local-to-global self-supervised learning framework that leverages unlabeled volumes by decomposing pretraining into intra-slice and inter-slice representation spaces. A slice encoder learns view-invariant local features, and a global encoder aggregates the resulting tokens to model volumetric context. The stop-gradient isolates the local space from the global objective, while slice-wise execution and a three-phase schedule support training under constrained GPU memory. On LIDC-IDRI lung nodule malignancy classification, L2GSSL reaches $0.9229$ AUROC with only $10\%$ of the labels and $0.9377$ with $25\%$, exceeding the volume-level VICReg by $0.0229$ and $0.0294$, respectively. With all labels, the strongest supervised baseline exceeds L2GSSL by only $0.0044$ AUROC, consistent with self-supervised pretraining providing its greatest value when annotations are limited. Without adaptation to the external LNDb cohort, a model fine-tuned on $25\%$ of LIDC-IDRI obtains $0.8138$ AUROC and $0.7589$ AUPRC, improving over the strongest evaluated self-supervised baseline by $0.1130$ and $0.0954$. Experiments across data sources, thoracic and abdominal anatomy, downstream tasks, and two backbones examine healthcare-data variety, while lesion-slice masking shows that the predictions depend on lesion-bearing content.

title: A Decision-Aware Evaluation Protocol for Uncertainty in Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Medical segmentation uncertainty is often evaluated with calibration error or pixel-level error-detection scores, but these metrics do not show whether uncertainty improves downstream review decisions. We propose a decision-aware evaluation protocol that separates uncertainty estimation from deferral policy and evaluates their combination under fixed review budgets: which pixels, regions, or images should be accepted, and which should be reviewed. The protocol reports fixed-budget error reduction, risk-coverage behaviour, region-level review proxies, structural failure modes, probability-derived baselines, and sensitivity to review assumptions. We instantiate it across retinal vessel, skin lesion, and polyp segmentation with multiple backbones and uncertainty estimators. Under matched inference budgets and canonical multi-layer MC Dropout, test-time augmentation (TTA) gives a stronger error-detection signal across matched MC--TTA comparisons, including architecture and dropout-placement checks. However, estimator rankings are not universal. For example, probability-derived scores remain competitive, deep ensembles can outperform TTA, learned deferral helps mainly when the base estimator is weak, and rankings can change with review unit, uncertainty target, correction assumptions, and cost model. Structural and second-observer analyses further show that boundary and thin-structure failures are partly tied to annotation ambiguity. These findings support evaluating uncertainty as an estimator-policy-review configuration, not as a standalone score map. title: Bridging the Markerless Tracking Validation Gap: Intraoperative X-ray Workflow Integration
abstract: Markerless intraoperative tracking of spinal anatomy via RGB-D sensors is a promising alternative to invasive bone-anchored fiducials, yet no existing clinical dataset provides independent subsurface ground truth for validating these methods. We address this gap with a clinically viable pipeline that derives per-vertebra 6-DoF pose from routine intraoperative C-arm fluoroscopy, co-registered to the RGB-D camera frame through a multimodal fiducial array detectable in both imaging modalities. Critically, the pipeline requires no additional radiation, instrumentation, or deviation from standard surgical workflows, relying solely on the fluoroscopic images already acquired during routine level checks. A calibrated transform chain links the vertebral pose recovered via multi-view 2D-3D CT-to-fluoroscopy registration to the RGB-D coordinate frame, enabling direct comparison of any markerless registration estimate against a subsurface reference. Ex vivo validation against optically tracked ovine vertebrae confirms end-to-end accuracy of 2.06 +- 0.29 mm and 3.35 +- 0.93 degrees, sufficient to serve as independent ground truth for methods with substantially larger errors. We demonstrate the pipeline's utility by evaluating two markerless registration strategies on clinical data spanning 11 vertebrae across 1,500 frames from three surgical sequences: the first such evaluation against an independent subsurface reference in a clinical setting. The proposed framework provides reusable infrastructure for benchmarking emerging markerless tracking methods on real surgical data.

title: Mixture of Multi-Sequence Feature Difference for Contrast-Enhanced MRI Synthesis
abstract: Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (CE-MRI) is crucial for accurately diagnosing and segmenting brain tumors. However, the acquisition of CE-MRI requires injecting contrast agents, which poses potential health risks and increases scan costs. Here, we propose a CE-MRI synthesis method from non-contrast sequences, reducing both risk and cost. Unlike existing methods that rely on channel-wise concatenation to fuse multi-sequence information for synthesis, we introduce a Mixture of Feature Difference (MoFD) module. The proposed module uses a dynamic weighting strategy to adaptively select and aggregate informative features from both individual source sequences and explicit differences among them. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms baselines in terms of image fidelity and perceptual quality on the UCSF-PDGM and UPenn-GBM datasets. Our method successfully reconstructs tumor regions and achieves segmentation performance comparable to that obtained with real CE-MRI. Our ablation studies show that although adversarial learning improves perceptual quality, a regression-based variant of our method achieves higher structural fidelity.

title: MedPAO-VL: Interpretable and Protocol-Compliant Agent for Structured Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Despite the remarkable generalization capabilities of Large Language Models, generating clinically accurate and structured radiology reports from medical images remains a significant challenge. Current end-to-end approaches function as black boxes, prone to factual hallucinations and generating ungrounded findings. This lack of reliability and failure to adhere to domain-specific structuring protocols, fundamentally limits their clinical utility. We present MedPAO-VL, a multimodal agent that shifts the paradigm from monolithic generation to explainable, iterative, protocol-compliant structured report generation. Unlike deterministic models, our plan-act-observe loop functions as a goal-oriented agent: it first perceives the Chest X-Ray through an explainable vision module designed to capture inherent diagnostic uncertainty, then iteratively refines the generated report by observing semantic discrepancies and self-correcting its generation for better alignment with visually detected clinical findings. Evaluation of our framework demonstrates that this agentic reasoning improves clinical correctness and completeness, achieving an expert-rated accuracy score of 3.5/5 and a structural score of 4.3/5. By prioritizing pathology specific explainability and iterative refinement over opaque end-to-end mapping, MedPAO-VL offers a transparent and clinically viable alternative for automated structured radiology report generation.

title: From Adults to Children: Benchmarking Foundation Models for Chest X-Ray Classification under Domain Shift
abstract: Foundation models have shown significant potential across diverse fields and have been applied to medical imaging, but their robustness across patient populations remains unclear. In this work, we investigate foundation models' ability to generalize from adult to pediatric chest X-ray classification. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first benchmark to compare multiple foundation models under a common adult-to-pediatric evaluation setting while also analyzing the effect of adaptation depth. We harmonize VinDr-CXR and PediCXR into a five-label classification task and evaluate six foundation models and two CNN baselines. All models are adapted using adult data only and tested in both the in-domain and pediatric domains using linear probing, partial fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning. The benchmark reveals a clear and consistent trend: all models suffer a substantial performance degradation when transferred from adult to pediatric data, with drops exceeding 10 percentage points. While Macro-AUROC values reach approximately 92% on the adult test set, performance decreases to around 78% on the pediatric domain. Another important finding is that increasing the depth of adaptation does not significantly improve cross-population generalization. Moreover, strong in-domain performance does not translate into better performance on pediatric data.

title: SCCL-DT: Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning with Dual-Rule Teacher Distillation for Zero-Shot Chest X-Ray Diagnosis
abstract: Contrastive vision-language pre-training supports zero-shot chest X-ray diagnosis, but standard objectives treat every off-diagonal image-report pair in a batch as a negative. In radiology, recurring findings across patients mean that instance mismatch need not imply semantic incompatibility, creating false-negative supervision that we term a semantic conflict. A training-trace audit shows that pair-observations selected by the online mask used during training are enriched for report-derived finding agreement, although this proxy analysis does not establish clinical equivalence. Fixed thresholds can become miscalibrated as similarity distributions evolve, while soft reweighting leaves residual repulsive gradients. We therefore propose Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning (SCCL), which tracks modality-specific similarity distributions with exponential-moving-average (EMA) statistics, derives adaptive thresholds, and hard-masks flagged candidates before softmax normalization. Inclusive (OR) and consensus (AND) rules define two SCCL teachers, whose bidirectional cross-modal rankings are consolidated through standard distillation into a single deployable student, SCCL-DT. Across five public chest X-ray benchmarks, SCCL-DT achieves a mean zero-shot AUC of $0.850$, compared with $0.837$ for the strongest evaluated baseline in our comparison. Code will be made publicly available soon.

title: FPG-Seg: Annotation-free Retinal Vessel Topology Segmentation
abstract: State-of-the art approaches to retinal vessel segmentation typically require extensive annotations, a highly time-consuming process, reliant on clinical expertise. We present FPG-Seg, an annotation-free pipeline for retinal vessel segmentation combining classical vesselness filtering, Bayesian deep learning and topology-aware graph reconstruction to segment retinal vessel topology without manual labels. Tested across four widely used benchmark datasets for retinal vessel segmentation, FPG-Seg attains a clDice of $0.74{-}0.78$, representing $86{-}98\%$ of the performance of an equivalent fully-supervised baseline, despite using no manual annotations for training or hyperparameter tuning. As part of this work, we also provide, to our knowledge, the first performance benchmark of an annotation-free vessel segmentation method on FIVES.

title: CRUX: Clinical-Text Anchoring for Cross-Institutional CT-Pathology Fusion in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Survival Prediction
abstract: Accurate prognosis in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) benefits from integrating computed tomography (CT) and histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs), which capture complementary macroscopic and microscopic disease characteristics. Fusing these modalities is difficult: their features come from different pretrained foundation-model encoders and lack spatial correspondence, and both are sensitive to institution-specific acquisition and staining, causing multimodal models to overfit site-specific artifacts and generalize poorly. We present CRUX (CRoss-modal Unification via teXt anchoring), a fusion framework that uses clinical text---encoded by a biomedical language model---as an institution-invariant semantic anchor. Because clinical variables follow standardized classification systems, their embeddings occupy a representation space that is consistent across institutions, providing a stable reference frame for aligning heterogeneous imaging features. CRUX introduces a text-mediated cross-modal bridge in which CT- and pathology-derived text-query summaries exchange information within a compact text semantic space through a learnable hub token, avoiding direct image-space cross-attention that would propagate domain-specific artifacts. We evaluate on 2,157 NSCLC patients from five hospitals, holding out one hospital (N=446) entirely for external validation. CRUX attains an external concordance index (C-index) of 0.761, the highest among all unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal configurations. Notably, direct CT-WSI fusion degrades under distribution shift, whereas text anchoring restores and improves cross-institutional generalization. These results indicate that language-model-encoded clinical text is an effective structured prior for robust, generalizable multimodal cancer prognosis.

title: Really Need Recursion? Revisiting One-pass Registration with Multi-level Multi-space Contextual Guidance
abstract: Deformable image registration is a fundamental challenge in medical image analysis. Recent deep learning-based methods typically adopt either one-pass architectures that complete registration in a single network iteration, or recursive architectures that refine registration through multiple passes. While recursive methods often improve accuracy, they incur substantial computational overhead and slower inference speed. In this paper, we challenge the necessity of recursion for high-performance deformable registration and propose M2CG, a one-pass registration network with Multi-level Multi-space Contextual Guidance. It performs multi-step progressive pyramid registration within a single iteration, guided at each step by contextual cues from three levels (previous, current, and subsequent steps) and four spaces (image space, image feature space, segmentation space, and segmentation feature space). Our M2CG supports both unsupervised (without any labels) and semi-supervised (with segmentation labels for partial training data) registration, and has achieved state-of-the-art performance across two well-benchmarked inter-/intra-patient medical registration tasks with eight public datasets. Our findings suggest that the current reliance on recursion may stem from the absence of sufficient contextual cues that comprehensively characterize the remaining distance to the target alignment.

title: CF-NODE: Counterfactual Spatial Node Intervention for Test-Time Adaptation Under Domain Shift, Evaluated Across Five Diabetic Retinopathy Datasets
abstract: Automated fundus-based diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading can substantially expand screening capacity, but source-trained models degrade sharply across different cameras, clinics, and patient populations. Existing test-time adaptation methods depend on entropy minimization or target information accumulated from image batches and streams. These mechanisms can reinforce confidently incorrect predictions and break down when clinical images arrive independently. We introduce CF-NODE, a novel counterfactual test-time adaptation framework for cross- domain DR grading. Instead of trusting prediction confidence or estimating a target distribution, CF-NODE asks how each prediction responds under a controlled intervention on the evidence supporting it. CF-NODE ranks internal spatial nodes using model-derived attention, feature magnitude, and node-set similarity, progressively attenuates the highest-ranked nodes, and uses the stability of the resulting expected-grade response to apply a bounded calibration of the predicted grade distribution. The framework is fully frozen and adapts every image independently using only geometric views and a fixed source-derived prior, requiring no target-derived information or model updates. We evaluate CF-NODE on five external DR datasets under repeated-seed evaluation against TENT, EATA, SAR, and T3A. CF-NODE outperforms all four methods with statistically significant improvements over the second-best method, improves AUC on every target domain, and attains the highest average AUC and macro-F1, delivering stronger grade discrimination together with more balanced recognition across DR severity levels. These results demonstrate that counterfactual intervention sensitivity provides consistent and deployment-ready domain robustness for single-image clinical inference.

title: LGGS: Longitudinal MRI Reconstruction via Guided Group Sparsity
abstract: Serial MRI is routinely performed in current clinical practice for disease surveillance and applications such as MR-guided radiotherapy. However, long MRI scan times increase costs and limit patient access, making accelerated image reconstruction of broad clinical importance. Previous scans of the same patient contain image information highly correlated with the current exam, yet existing reconstruction methods rarely exploit this information. Major challenges in the effective use of prior scans include inter-visit misregistration, pathological changes, and image phase variation. In this work, we propose Longitudinal Guided Group Sparsity (LGGS), an interpretable deep-learning framework for longitudinally informed MRI reconstruction derived from classical group sparsity. The prior scan is incorporated into the reconstruction regularizer through learned phase-invariant circulant attention that identifies corresponding features across exams. This formulation provides robustness to local in-plane and through-plane misregistration as well as inter-visit phase variation. Across acceleration rates, LGGS achieves state-of-the-art performance on longitudinal T1-weighted multi-coil brain MRI data, outperforming the evaluated unguided and longitudinally informed reconstruction methods, with substantially fewer learned parameters. We further evaluated the contributions of multiple guide slices and phase-invariant similarity and demonstrated that accelerated prior images can also serve as effective guides with minimal degradation in reconstruction quality.

title: HilbertGen-3D:Hilbert--Multifractal Conditioning for Topology-Aware 3D Generation
abstract: High-fidelity 3D generative modeling underpins game asset creation, medical imaging, and VR/AR environmental design, where geometric structure directly influences perception and decision-making. Diffusion models represent a powerful paradigm for point cloud generation. However, existing approaches rely heavily on local voxel or patch features and often miss global structural organization, and much less work has studied how global conditioning can be used to improve generation quality. In this paper, we introduce HilbertGen-3D, a novel topology-aware conditional diffusion framework based on Hilbert-Multifractal Conditioning (HMC). HMC computes multi-scale voxel measures, serializes them via a 3D Hilbert curve to expose structured spatial dependencies, and estimates the generalized fractal dimensions from scale-dependent partition functions. We encode these signals as global embeddings and multi-scale tokens, and inject them into a diffusion denoiser through an efficient bottleneck fusion module. Across the Chair, Airplane, and Car categories of ShapeNet, our two conditioning variants reduce the absolute deviation of 1-Nearest Neighbor Accuracy (1-NNA) from 50% by up to 8.90 percentage points and increase coverage by up to 5.88 percentage points relative to TopoDiT-3D. This shows that combining local density cues with global Hilbert-multifractal structure provides a simple and effective recipe for high-fidelity and diverse 3D generation.

title: MedSTP: Preserving Subspace and Transition Evidence for Medical VQA Token Pruning
abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) for visual question answering (VQA) often pass long visual-token sequences to the language model, making visual-token pruning attractive but risky for medical images, where answers may depend on localized boundary and texture evidence. We study training free pre-decoding pruning and treat pruning as a subspace stable evidence preservation problem. The retained tokens should remain close to the dominant visual evidence subspace induced by the full token set. To this end, we propose \emph{Subspace-Transition Token Pruning} (\method{}), which estimates each token's spectral support from principal component space and constructs a compact representation subspace. To better reflect medical image structure, \method{} further uses a bounded token-grid transition prior to promote boundary and texture sensitive tokens. We evaluate \method{} on the closed-ended SLAKE and OmniMedVQA benchmarks and on RadImageNet-VQA, which provides both closed-ended and open-ended evaluations, using Lingshu-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B backbones. \method{} delivers consistently strong performance on both the closed-ended and open-ended RadImageNet-VQA evaluations. These results show that \method{} is an effective training free pruning framework for medical domain VQA.

title: An Anatomy-Aware Staged Pipeline for Vessel-Specific Intracranial Aneurysm Segmentation in CT and MR Angiography
abstract: The TopAneu 2026 challenge requires intracranial aneurysms to be segmented at the voxel level and assigned to one of more than fifty vessel-specific classes, on CT and MR angiography alike. We address it with a six-stage anatomy-aware pipeline rather than a single segmentation network. A logistic-regression classifier routes each scan to a modality-specific branch; networks segment the vasculature, first as a binary mask and then over the full 36-class arterial taxonomy; a candidate localiser turns raw angiography and vessel priors into suspicious regions; a candidate-centred network segments the lesion in each crop; connected components become instances; and a per-instance classifier assigns each its anatomical location. Two principles organise the design. Whenever an upstream model output becomes a downstream training input it is generated out-of-fold, so no stage trains on unrealistically clean predictions of itself. And the anatomical decision is made once per lesion rather than once per voxel, which fits the data: of 406 connected aneurysm components in the full release, 405 carry exactly one location label. Task 1 is read off the Task 2 mask, making the two consistent by construction. We report stage-wise performance and a five-part ablation isolating what vessel priors and class-aware sampling contribute at each stage.

title: Clinician Use of an Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Clinical Information Platform.
abstract: Importance Despite growing interest in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in medicine, empirical evidence on how clinicians use these tools is limited. Objective To characterize clinician use of an AI-enabled clinical information platform, the distribution of use across the clinical workforce, and the purpose of submitted queries. Design, setting, and participants This cross-sectional study analyzed clinicians with National Provider Identifier-verified accounts of a commonly used AI-enabled clinical information platform, OpenEvidence, from January 1, 2024, through June 30, 2026. A large language model was used to classify the clinical purpose and topic areas of a stratified random sample of 38.8 million queries. Main outcomes and measures The number of active users and clinical queries, the share of queries relative to representation in the national workforce, and the clinical purpose and topic of queries were examined. Results Overall, 952 008 clinicians (58.5% female), including 556 200 physicians, submitted 271 million queries during the 2.5-year study period. Monthly active users increased from 355 in January 2024 to 703 265 in June 2026, and average monthly queries per active user rose from 18.0 to 39.5. Nurse practitioners (44.5) and physician assistants (44.5) submitted more queries per active user-month than physicians (37.1). A higher share of queries relative to the national workforce was submitted by physicians within a decade of graduation (use ratio, 2.54) and residents and fellows (1.84). Use was also higher than average among physicians specializing in oncology and hematology (use ratio, 2.00), internal medicine (1.88), and family medicine (1.80), but lower in procedural and diagnostic specialties (ophthalmology, 0.23; radiology, 0.24; orthopedics, 0.24). Most queries addressed clinical decision-making (51.9%), particularly treatment and management (33.1%), whereas diagnosis accounted for 13.9% of queries. Queries addressing topics outside physicians' own specialties ranged from 35% among oncologists and hematologists to 88% among emergency department physicians. Conclusions and relevance Over 2.5 years, more than 950 000 US clinicians submitted greater than 270 million queries to an AI-enabled clinical information platform. Use varied across clinician types, specialties, and career stages and was frequently for treatment decisions rather than diagnostic tasks.

title: Neoadjuvant Stereotactic Ablative Radiotherapy Before Inferior Vena Cava Thrombectomy for Renal Cell Carcinoma: A Phase 2 Nonrandomized Clinical Trial.
abstract: Importance Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) with inferior vena cava (IVC) tumor thrombus is associated with substantial perioperative risk and frequent recurrence despite nephrectomy and thrombectomy. No established neoadjuvant local therapy exists for this high-risk population. Objective To evaluate the feasibility, safety, clinical outcomes, and exploratory biomarker effects of neoadjuvant stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR) targeting IVC tumor thrombus before nephrectomy and thrombectomy. Design, setting, and participants This single-center prospective phase 2 nonrandomized clinical trial enrolled patients with newly diagnosed RCC and Mayo level II to IV IVC tumor thrombus eligible for neoadjuvant SABR and definitive surgery from July 2015 to January 2024. Data were analyzed from August 2025 to August 2026. Intervention Neoadjuvant SABR to the radiographically defined IVC tumor thrombus, delivered as 40 Gy in 5 fractions or 36 Gy in 3 fractions, followed by radical nephrectomy and IVC thrombectomy. Main outcomes and measures The primary end point was 1-year recurrence-free survival (RFS) compared with a prespecified historical surgery-alone benchmark of 55.7%. Secondary outcomes included 90-day perioperative morbidity and mortality, adverse events, pulmonary embolism, overall survival, and cancer-specific survival. Exploratory analyses included Ki-67 immunohistochemistry and tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA. Results Of 23 patients who received neoadjuvant SABR, 22 completed surgery, and 21 were included in the primary RFS analysis. Of 21 included patients, 12 (57%) were male, and the median (IQR) age was 62.5 (54.0-73.2) years. A total of 19 patients had clear-cell RCC; all tumors were grade 3 or 4, and 3 patients had metastatic disease at enrollment. At a median (range) follow-up of 108.6 (2.0-127.2) months, 1-year RFS was 71.4% (80% CI, 56.6-82.0; 95% CI, 47.2-86.0), meeting the prespecified phase 2 screening criterion based on comparison with the historical surgery-alone benchmark of 55.7% (P = .09). One-year overall survival was 95.2% (80% CI, 83.9-98.7; 95% CI, 70.7-99.3) and cancer-specific survival was 95.2% (80% CI, 83.9-98.7; 95% CI, 70.7-99.3). No 90-day perioperative mortality occurred; 4 grade 4 treatment-attributed events occurred, but no grade 4/5 radiation-attributed toxic effects occurred. Ki-67 expression was reduced in patients with irradiated tumor thrombus compared with nonirradiated controls. Tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA was detected in all patients with available plasma and declined after treatment. Conclusions and relevance In this nonrandomized clinical trial, neoadjuvant SABR before nephrectomy and IVC thrombectomy appeared feasible with an acceptable safety profile. RFS met the prespecified phase 2 screening criterion but remains exploratory and warrants further evaluation. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02473536.

No 90-day perioperative mortality occurred; 4 grade 4 treatment-attributed events occurred, but no grade 4/5 radiation-attributed toxic effects occurred. Ki-67 expression was reduced in patients with irradiated tumor thrombus compared with nonirradiated controls. Tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA was detected in all patients with available plasma and declined after treatment.

Conclusions and relevance

In this nonrandomized clinical trial, neoadjuvant SABR before nephrectomy and IVC thrombectomy appeared feasible with an acceptable safety profile. RFS met the prespecified phase 2 screening criterion but remains exploratory and warrants further evaluation.

Trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT02473536.

title: Primary Pure Yolk Sac Tumor of the Urinary Bladder: A Case Report.
abstract: Introduction Yolk sac tumors are malignant germ cell tumors that typically arise in the gonads. Although extragonadal cases have been reported, primary involvement of the urinary tract is extremely rare. Case presentation A 67-year-old man presented with gross hematuria. Cystoscopy and contrast-enhanced computed tomography revealed a 6-cm bladder mass. Transurethral resection of the bladder tumor was performed. Histopathological and immunohistochemical findings (alpha-fetoprotein, glypican-3, and Sal-like protein 4 positivity) were consistent with a yolk sac tumor without a urothelial carcinoma component. Additional examinations revealed no primary lesions elsewhere, leading to the diagnosis of a primary bladder yolk sac tumor. The patient received four cycles of etoposide and cisplatin chemotherapy and has remained recurrence-free for 2 years. Conclusions Patients with primary bladder yolk sac tumors, although rare, may achieve favorable outcomes with combined surgical resection and chemotherapy.

Additional examinations revealed no primary lesions elsewhere, leading to the diagnosis of a primary bladder yolk sac tumor. The patient received four cycles of etoposide and cisplatin chemotherapy and has remained recurrence-free for 2 years.

Conclusions

Patients with primary bladder yolk sac tumors, although rare, may achieve favorable outcomes with combined surgical resection and chemotherapy.

title: Artificial intelligence across the continuum of care for the aging musculoskeletal patient: From longitudinal phenotyping to personalized surgery and recovery monitoring.
abstract: Musculoskeletal care is being reshaped by population aging, multimorbidity, frailty, osteoporosis, sarcopenia, polypharmacy and increasing vulnerability to postoperative loss of independence. Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered orthopaedic research, but its clinical translation remains constrained. Many models address isolated diagnostic, imaging or short-term prediction tasks rather than the longitudinal care trajectories that determine outcomes in older musculoskeletal patients. The central limitation is therefore not simply whether older adults are represented in datasets, but whether AI systems are valid across the continuum of geriatric orthopaedic care. This review argues for a transition from task-specific orthopaedic AI toward continuum-of-care AI for the aging musculoskeletal patient. Upstream, radiomics, longitudinal osteoarthritis phenotyping, opportunistic computed tomography (CT)-based skeletal assessment and AI-augmented dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) modelling may improve prediction of disease progression, fracture risk, treatment failure and surgical timing. At the point of intervention, AI-assisted arthroplasty planning may help move total knee arthroplasty from generic alignment targets toward phenotype-specific reconstruction strategies that account for constitutional alignment, bone morphology, ligament envelope, neuromuscular control, frailty and functional reserve. Perioperatively, automated frailty and sarcopenia phenotyping, wearable gait analysis and multimodal temporal models integrating imaging, electronic health records, laboratory data, medications, patient-reported outcomes and wearable signals may support dynamic risk prediction. After discharge, continuous monitoring of mobility, sleep, pain trajectories, wound-related symptoms and rehabilitation adherence may help close the high-risk surveillance gap during the 90-day postoperative episode. However, clinical adoption requires more than high discrimination. Explainable AI should be understood as one component of a broader trust framework that also includes calibration, uncertainty quantification, decision-curve analysis, external and prospective validation, workflow integration, post-deployment monitoring and accountability. The future of orthopaedic AI is not simply better diagnosis or more precise surgery, but longitudinal, multimodal support across the full care continuum: predicting progression, selecting treatment, personalizing surgery, optimizing perioperative care, monitoring recovery and preserving mobility and independence. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV.

title: Response to the Correspondence Regarding "Cutaneous Metastasis From Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma Eight Years After Initial Surgery".
abstract: We sincerely thank Dr. Sengul and colleagues for their insightful comments on our case report of skin metastasis in papillary thyroid cancer (PTC). They questioned the adequacy of local excision and suggested completion thyroidectomy to enable radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy or systemic therapy. We appreciate their perspective but explain our rationale, given the exceptional rarity of isolated cutaneous metastasis and limited evidence-based guidelines. Complete surgical excision may be appropriate for carefully selected patients with solitary cutaneous metastasis, whereas RAI or systemic therapy should be considered according to disease extent, iodine avidity, tumor biology, and patient-specific factors. We agree that TSH suppression alone does not explain the development of metastasis and that TERT promoter mutations may provide additional insight into the aggressive biological behavior of PTC. Despite the loss of thyroglobulin (Tg) expression in the metastasis, our multimodal surveillance-including ultrasonography and CT-has shown no recurrence, and we will offer functional imaging when clinical indicated. No evidence of recurrent or additional metastatic disease during follow-up, and per 2025 ATA guidelines, shared decision-making favored thyroid preservation with close follow-up. Future disease progression would prompt reconsideration of total thyroidectomy with RAI or targeted therapy.

title: [Enteral contrast media-when, what, and how?]
abstract: Background Enteral contrast media (CM) administration in abdominal computed tomography (CT) is handled inconsistently across Germany. Objective To present the current recommendations on enteral CM administration based on the key questions of when, what, and how, and to translate them into radiological practice. Materials and methods Synthesis of indication-based recommendations, CM classes and their technical properties, and the practical execution of both routes of administration, based on the German Radiological Society (DRG) recommendations, current guidelines, published evidence, and institutional practice. Results Positive oral CM are obsolete for most abdominal indications-including acute abdomen, ileus, and trauma-and are contraindicated when gastrointestinal bleeding or ischemia is suspected. In suspected perforation, routine oral contrast should be omitted and barium sulfate is contraindicated, whereas water-soluble iodinated agents remain an option when a leak has to be demonstrated specifically. Furthermore, enteral contrast with neutral oral CM remains useful for upper gastrointestinal tumor staging and enterography (preferably magnetic resonance enterography). Conclusion Indication-appropriate, guideline-based enteral contrast administration reduces unnecessary burden without compromising diagnostic accuracy and should be embedded in standardized workflows.
originalAbstract:
Background

Enteral contrast media (CM) administration in abdominal computed tomography (CT) is handled inconsistently across Germany.

Objective

To present the current recommendations on enteral CM administration based on the key questions of when, what, and how, and to translate them into radiological practice.

Materials and methods

Synthesis of indication-based recommendations, CM classes and their technical properties, and the practical execution of both routes of administration, based on the German Radiological Society (DRG) recommendations, current guidelines, published evidence, and institutional practice.

Results

Positive oral CM are obsolete for most abdominal indications-including acute abdomen, ileus, and trauma-and are contraindicated when gastrointestinal bleeding or ischemia is suspected. In suspected perforation, routine oral contrast should be omitted and barium sulfate is contraindicated, whereas water-soluble iodinated agents remain an option when a leak has to be demonstrated specifically. Furthermore, enteral contrast with neutral oral CM remains useful for upper gastrointestinal tumor staging and enterography (preferably magnetic resonance enterography).

Conclusion

Indication-appropriate, guideline-based enteral contrast administration reduces unnecessary burden without compromising diagnostic accuracy and should be embedded in standardized workflows.

title: Sylviocentral ratio: a novel magnetic resonance imaging marker for differentiating probable idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus from diffuse cerebral atrophy.
abstract: Probable idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus (pNPH) is a potentially treatable neurological disorder that can be difficult to differentiate from diffuse cerebral atrophy because of overlapping clinical and imaging features. This study evaluated the diagnostic performance of a novel magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived marker, the sylviocentral ratio, for distinguishing pNPH from diffuse cerebral atrophy. In this prospective study, 72 patients (36 with pNPH and 36 with diffuse cerebral atrophy) underwent routine brain MRI, with an additional sagittal 3D T2-weighted SPACE acquisition; axial and coronal reformatted images were generated from the volumetric dataset for standardized measurements. Sylvian fissure and central sulcus diameters were measured on these standardized images using predefined anatomical landmarks, and the sylviocentral ratio was calculated. The sylviocentral ratio was significantly higher in patients with pNPH than in those with diffuse cerebral atrophy (10.94 ± 4.67 vs. 2.86 ± 2.00, p < 0.001). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance, with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.953 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.896-0.994). A cut-off value of ≥ 5.3 yielded a sensitivity of 91.7% and a specificity of 94.4%. Diagnostic performance was comparable to the callosal angle (AUC = 0.951) and superior to the Evans index (AUC = 0.922). The sylviocentral ratio remained independently associated with pNPH after adjustment for age (p < 0.001). Interobserver agreement was excellent (intraclass correlation coefficient [ICC] = 0.94). The sylviocentral ratio is a practical, reproducible, and highly accurate MRI marker for differentiating pNPH from diffuse cerebral atrophy and may complement established imaging parameters in clinical assessment. Given the limited size of the age-matched cohort, validation in larger, ideally external cohorts is warranted before widespread clinical implementation.
